UNIT.subject: Biology
UNIT.strand: Strand 2.0: Anatomy and Physiology of Plants
UNIT.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
UNIT.content:
• Meaning and significance of growth and development
• Structure of the seed (monocots and dicots)
• Seed dormancy (meaning, significance, causes and ways of breaking seed dormancy)
• Germination (process, types and conditions necessary for germination)
• Primary and secondary growth
• Measurement of growth and growth curves
• Role of hormones in plant growth and development (include apical dominance)
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) distinguish between growth and development in living organisms,
b) relate structures of monocot and dicot seeds to their functions,
c) outline causes and ways of breaking dormancy in seeds,
d) investigate conditions necessary for seed germination,
e) investigate types of germination in plants,
f) illustrate primary and secondary growth in flowering plants,
g) demonstrate the role of hormones in plant growth and development,
h) appreciate the importance of growth and development in plants.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Citizenship: The learner solves problems in the community by sharing the seedlings from the established tree nursery.
• Learning to Learn: The learner reflects on their own work and adjusts accordingly while carrying out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: Learners investigate the farmer's problem of uneven germination and growth of maize and beans.
• Communication and Collaboration: Learners share evidence and findings in group investigations.
• Creativity and Imagination: Learners design experiments and build and revise models.
• Digital Literacy: Learners use the maize and bean time-lapse videos and other digital resources, with teacher-prepared alternatives where there is no connectivity.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: The learner works harmoniously with others while carrying out experiments to investigate conditions necessary for seed germination.
• Patriotism: The learner demonstrates devotion to the country/community while sharing seedlings with the school community for environmental conservation, and links healthy plant growth to Kenya's food security and agricultural development.
• Responsibility: Learners care for the experimental seeds and follow procedures.
• Integrity: Learners record actual observations rather than changing results to match predictions.
• Respect: Learners listen to and consider other learners' explanations.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions: Learners write questions after the time-lapse videos and post them on the Driving Question Board.
• Developing and Using Models: Learners draw initial models of maize and bean growth and revise them after each lesson, including models of secondary growth.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners test conditions for germination, types of germination and regions of growth using maize and bean seeds.
• Analyzing and Interpreting Data: Learners record seedling height or stem width and draw growth curves.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners explain differences in germination, emergence and growth using evidence on seed structure, dormancy, conditions and hormones.
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: Learners discuss and defend explanations with peers.
• Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information: Learners use readings, videos and animations on hormones and growth.
UNIT.pcis:
• Financial Literacy: The learner explores ways of generating income while selling seedlings to members of the community.
• Prevention of Global Warming: The learner mitigates the effects of global warming by establishing a tree nursery and distributing seedlings in the community.
• Food security and nutrition: Understanding germination and growth supports better maize and bean production.
• Climate change and adaptation: Rainfall and temperature affect germination and crop establishment.
• Sustainable agriculture, environmental conservation and water conservation: Use of resources in crop and seedling production.
• Technology and innovation: Use of hormones and time-lapse technology in agriculture.
UNIT.careers:
• Agronomist: How can farmers improve crop establishment and growth?
• Seed Technologist: Why do some seeds germinate while others fail to germinate?
• Agricultural Research Scientist: What conditions produce better germination and plant growth?
• Plant Physiologist: What processes and hormones control plant growth?
• Plant Breeder: Can varieties be developed that germinate and grow better under Kenyan conditions?
• Agricultural Extension Officer: How can this knowledge be transferred to farmers?
UNIT.focus: This unit uses the puzzle of uneven germination, emergence and growth in a farmer's maize and beans to drive learning about seed structure, dormancy, germination, primary and secondary growth, growth measurement and hormones. Learners start with time-lapse videos, predict, investigate with locally available seeds in small groups, and revise a cumulative model each lesson. The unit ends in a tree nursery project in which stem cuttings are rooted using natural hormone sources such as bulb onions, Aloe and cinnamon.
UNIT.phenomenon: A farmer plants maize and beans on the same day after rainfall. Some seeds germinate within a few days, while others take longer. Some seeds fail to germinate even though they appear healthy. As the plants grow, the stems become taller and thicker, roots extend deeper, and some plants develop branches. Learners first watch time-lapse videos of a bean seedling and a maize seedling germinating and growing, so they see the process before explaining it. It is puzzling because the seeds were planted on the same day, in the same field, with the same rain, yet they behave very differently. Healthy-looking seeds do not germinate, maize and beans emerge differently, and growth is not just getting taller since stems also thicken and branch. What explains these differences?
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Time-lapse video: Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section, showing bean germination and root and shoot growth below and above the soil.
• Time-lapse video: Growing corn time lapse (#greentimelapse #gtl #timelapse), showing maize seedling germination and growth.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How does growth occur in plants?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1: The learner gets to know the phenomena. Watch the time-lapse videos of maize and beans (Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse), draw initial models, and write questions to post on the Driving Question Board. Question raised: What is growth and development?
Lesson 2: Meaning of growth and development. Structure of the seed (monocot and dicot). Discuss the meaning of growth and development, observe, draw and label monocot and dicot seeds, and discuss the functions of the structures with peers. Question raised: What is seed dormancy?
Lesson 3: Seed dormancy. Examine seed specimens to identify causes of seed dormancy and discuss with peers; carry out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy. Question raised: How does germination occur?
Lesson 4: Germination (process, types and conditions necessary for germination). Use maize and bean seeds to investigate conditions necessary for germination and carry out experiments to investigate types of germination. Question raised: How do plants show growth?
Lesson 5: Primary and secondary growth. Observe stem sections under a microscope, draw and label them, and use drawings and models to illustrate stages of secondary growth. Question raised: How can you measure growth in plants?
Lesson 6: Measurement of growth and growth curves. Use seedlings to determine regions of growth, record data, draw growth curves and discuss regions of growth with peers. Question raised: Do we have hormones in plants?
Lesson 7: Role of hormones in plant growth and development. Watch a video on the effect of plant hormones, read about the roles and functions of plant hormones (including apical dominance), and revise the model to explain the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and beans.
Lesson 8: Apply the hormone ideas to the tree nursery project by rooting stem cuttings with natural hormone sources (bulb onions, Aloe, cinnamon).
Lesson 9: Consolidate the evidence from all lessons, finalise the cumulative model and explanation for the farmer's maize and beans, and review the Driving Question Board.
Lesson 10: Present the final models and explanations, reflect on learning, and plan sharing and selling of seedlings to the community for conservation and income.

LESSONS.title: Meeting the Phenomenon: Mr. Wafula's Maize and Beans
LESSONS.duration: 80 minutes (double lesson); can be split into 2 x 40 minutes
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: phenomenon, germination, emergence, growth, time-lapse, initial model, Driving Question Board, maize H614, bean Rosecoco

slo.purpose: To launch the unit by letting learners meet the phenomenon: maize H614 and bean Rosecoco planted on the same day, in the same field, after the same rain on Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale, yet they germinate, emerge and grow differently. Learners observe, describe, draw their first models and post their questions on the Driving Question Board.
slo.knowledge: Learners describe differences in germination, emergence and growth between maize and beans using the time-lapse events and Day 14 counts: Maize radicle Day 4, emergence Day 7, first leaf Day 10; Bean radicle Day 3, emergence Day 8, first true leaves Day 12, branching by Day 25. Maize 88 of 100 and beans 80 of 100 germinated by Day 14. Maize is taller from Day 14 onward. Learners recognise that growth is more than getting taller (stems also thicken and branch) and that healthy-looking seeds can fail to germinate.
slo.skills: Observing and recording from a time-lapse video; comparing two sets of data; drawing and labelling an initial model; asking testable scientific questions; communicating ideas in simple, clear scientific English (SEP: Developing and Using Models; Asking Questions; Analyzing and Interpreting Data).
slo.attitudes: Curiosity about how crops grown by Kenyan farmers develop; willingness to share tentative ideas without fear of being wrong (Unity); respect for peers' ideas. Core competency: Learning to Learn, where the learner reflects on their own work and adjusts accordingly. PCI link: Financial Literacy, since a farmer's seed losses affect income.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson. It builds on no earlier lesson. It sets the puzzle, records learners' baseline ideas and opens the DQB. The question it raises for Lesson 2 is: What is growth and development? Lesson 2 will then teach definitions and seed structure, so they are not taught here.
slo.safetyNotes: Handle seeds with clean hands; some commercial maize seed is treated with fungicide and must not be put in the mouth, so wash hands after handling. Keep walkways clear when learners move to the DQB. If the class is large, use groups of 5 to 6 and share one screen or the teacher's printed stills. If no electricity or internet is available, use the teacher-prepared still-image strips and the events table described below.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens with a story: Mr. Wafula, a farmer near Kitale in Trans-Nzoia, planted maize H614 and Rosecoco beans on the same day (Day 0), 3 cm deep, after 25 mm of rain. Yet some seeds came up quickly, some slowly and some never germinated even though they looked healthy. Learners first predict and sketch their initial ideas, then watch the two time-lapse videos (Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse) and record what they see in an events table. They are shown the Day 14 germination counts (maize 88/100, beans 80/100) and the height trend (maize taller from Day 14 onward). Using Think-Pair-Share they draw an initial model and complete sentence starters. The teacher does not mark these as right or wrong. In groups, learners write questions on sticky notes or cards and post them on the Driving Question Board, grouping them into categories. The lesson ends with an exit ticket and the class question for Lesson 2: What is growth and development? If there is no power, the teacher uses a prepared strip of 6 labelled sketches per crop (Day 0, 3/4, 7/8, 10/12, 17/18, 25) and reads the events table aloud.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners listen to the farmer's problem: Mr. Wafula near Kitale planted maize H614 and Rosecoco beans on the same day, 3 cm deep, after 25 mm of rain, in the same field. Individually (2 min) they draw what they think happens to one maize seed and one bean seed after planting, showing root and shoot, and complete: 'I think maize and bean plants grow differently because...' and 'I think a seed needs ________ in order to germinate because...'. They then share with a partner (3 min) and a few pairs share with the class (Think-Pair-Share). The drawings are kept in their books as Day 1 baseline models.
framework.teacherMoves: Read the story slowly and show a real maize grain and a dry bean seed (or pictures). Say: 'Same day, same field, same rain. What do you think will happen to these seeds?' Give 2 minutes of silent individual WAIT TIME, then say: 'Turn to your partner and compare your drawings.' Circulate and listen for ideas such as 'beans need more water' or 'maize is stronger'; note them without correcting. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) to share a partner's idea, saying: 'Wanjiru, tell us what your partner drew.' After each answer give 10 to 15 seconds of WAIT TIME before the next. Say clearly: 'I will not mark these right or wrong. These are your first ideas and we will return to them at the end of the unit.' Clarify words such as germinate (seed starts to grow) in simple English.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with Predict-Observe-Explain (the 'Predict' step): committing to a prediction in writing before seeing evidence makes learners' prior ideas visible to themselves and to the teacher, so later evidence can confirm or challenge them. Cold-calling the partner's idea builds listening and safe sharing.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: tick learners who (a) draw both seeds, (b) show root and shoot, (c) add at least 2 labels or arrows, (d) complete both sentence starters. Look for common baseline ideas or misconceptions (e.g. 'all healthy seeds will germinate', 'growth means only getting taller', 'beans and maize germinate in the same way') and record them on a class list. No marks are given; this is a baseline.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners watch the two time-lapse videos (Bean Time-Lapse - 25 days | Soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse), each played twice. In the first viewing they just watch. In the second viewing, in groups of 5 to 6, they fill a simple events table: radicle appears (germination), shoot appears above soil (emergence), first leaf, branching. Then they study the farm data: events table (Bean: radicle Day 3, emergence Day 8, first true leaves Day 12, trifoliate leaves Day 18, branching by Day 25; Maize: radicle Day 4, emergence Day 7, first leaf Day 10, 3 leaves Day 17, seed food store stays underground), Day 14 germination counts out of 100 seeds (maize 88 germinated, 12 did not; beans 80 germinated, 20 did not), and the height trend (maize taller than beans from Day 14 onward). Learners complete 'I notice that...' and 'I wonder why...' statements, noting that some seeds that looked healthy did not germinate, and that stems also thicken and branch.
framework.teacherMoves: Before playing, say: 'Watch for three things: when the root appears, when the shoot comes above the soil, and what changes besides height.' Play each video twice; pause at key moments and ask: 'What do you see happening right now?' with 10 to 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 groups to report one observation each. Write the class's observations on the board in two columns, Maize and Bean. Then display or hand out the events table and Day 14 counts. Ask: 'Which crop germinated more seeds by Day 14? How many seeds did not germinate in each?' (12 and 20.) Ask: 'Which emerged first, maize or beans?' (Maize, Day 7 versus Day 8, although the bean radicle came first, Day 3 versus Day 4.) Ask: 'If the rain and planting day were the same, what could be different?' and give 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Do not explain causes; say: 'Hold on to that thought; we will investigate it.' If there is no power, use the prepared sketch strips and read the events table aloud, asking learners to arrange the sketches in order.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the 'Observe' step) with structured noticing: a table forces learners to compare the same events (germination, emergence, leaves) across both crops, moving them from vague impressions ('beans are slower') to specific, data-based observations. Separating 'what I notice' from 'what I wonder' keeps description apart from explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probing: ask 'How do you know the bean germinated before it emerged?' Listen for use of radicle versus shoot above soil. Check each group's events table: Are Day numbers correct (e.g. maize emergence Day 7, bean Day 8)? Do learners state the counts correctly (88 and 80)? Look for learners who note that growth includes thickening and branching, not only height. Record misconceptions such as confusing germination and emergence.

framework.learnerExperience: Individually, learners revise their drawing into an initial model that explains the farmer's puzzle: they draw a maize seed and a bean seed in the soil, show what happens after planting, show the root and shoot emerging at different times, and show how the plant develops over time. They add arrows and labels and write a short initial explanation using sentence starters: 'I think the seeds differ because...' and 'I think some healthy-looking seeds do not germinate because...'. In pairs they then use Claim-Evidence-Reasoning in a light form: claim (e.g. 'Maize and beans grow differently'), evidence from the table or counts (e.g. 'Maize emerged Day 7, beans Day 8; maize 88, beans 80'), and a tentative reason. A few learners present their models.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Draw what you think is happening that we cannot see inside the soil. Use arrows and labels.' Give 5 minutes of silent work and 10 to 15 seconds WAIT TIME before taking questions. Circulate and ask: 'What does this arrow show?' and 'What evidence from the video or table supports this part?' Select 3 contrasting models (not the 'best') for sharing, and cold-call 2 other learners to say one thing they like about each model and one thing they are unsure about. Emphasise: 'Models are drafts. They will change.' Display a few models on the wall. Do not supply the scientific explanation; accept ideas such as water, soil, seed type, seed age, pests and oxygen, and record them on the board as 'possible factors to test'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model-based reasoning with Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: drawing an initial model forces learners to turn observations into a mechanism, exposing gaps (such as what is inside the seed). Linking claims to specific evidence from the events table and counts starts the habit of evidence-based explanation that is used in every later lesson. Peer comments are a first form of peer review.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a model check: look for evidence that the model (a) shows both seeds, (b) shows root and shoot, (c) shows change over time, (d) has labels and arrows, (e) offers at least one reason for the differences. Collect 5 to 6 models to photocopy or keep for revision at the end of the unit. Note the most common ideas for later lessons. Peer feedback quality: do learners point to evidence rather than opinion?

framework.learnerExperience: In small groups, learners discuss: 'What questions do you have after watching the videos and considering the farmer's problem?' Each group writes at least 3 questions on sticky notes or cards (e.g. Wanjiru-style questions: 'Why did some healthy-looking seeds not germinate?', 'Why did maize emerge before beans?', 'Why did the bean plant branch but not the maize?', 'What is growth and development?'). They post the questions on the DQB under the driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants? As a class they cluster similar questions (seeds, conditions, growth, hormones) and choose the first question to follow up: What is growth and development?
framework.teacherMoves: Post the driving question at the top of the board or a large manila paper. Say: 'Every question is welcome. Make it a question we could investigate.' Give groups 5 minutes and 10 to 15 seconds WAIT TIME after setting the task. Walk around and push on vague questions: 'Can you ask that so we could test it?' Invite 5 groups to come forward (cold-call, one at a time) to read and post one question and say where it should be clustered. Group the notes with the class under headings such as Seeds, Conditions, Growth and Branching, and Other. Point out the question appearing most often: 'Many of you asked what growth and development mean. That is where we begin in Lesson 2.' If there is no sticky note supply, use cut paper and flour paste or tape, or write on the chalkboard.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the Driving Question Board: turning curiosity into a visible, shared set of questions gives learners ownership of the inquiry and a way to connect every later lesson back to the main question. Clustering helps learners see patterns and decide what to investigate first.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check the quality of questions: tally how many are about causes (why/how) versus simple facts. Observe participation: does each group member contribute a question? Note whether learners connect questions to evidence from the videos or data. Identify questions needing refinement and ask learners to reword them. Record which DQB clusters appear so later lessons can return to them.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their Day 1 drawing and add a 'Questions I still have' box and one improvement they would like to make but cannot yet (e.g. 'I do not know what is inside the seed'). They file the model in their books as the baseline for revision, and they complete an exit ticket: 'What did we observe today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?' They also write one thing they now want to find out. A few learners share in a gallery-style quick walk where they look at 3 posted models and leave one question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Keep this model safe. You will change it when you have evidence.' Remind learners that being unsure is part of science. Hand out or have learners write exit tickets on a half-page. Circulate during the quick gallery walk and say: 'Leave one question on a model that you want its owner to think about.' Give 10 to 15 seconds WAIT TIME before closing questions. Cold-call 3 learners to read an exit ticket answer aloud. Close with: 'Today we saw that maize and beans, planted on the same day at Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale, behaved differently. Our new question is: What is growth and development? That is how we start Lesson 2.' Set optional home task: ask a parent or a farmer how they decide when a seed has failed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision (baseline step) and Gallery Walk: saving an initial model and naming what is missing creates the benchmark for revision later in the unit, and leaving questions on peers' models starts the culture of peer review. Exit tickets link the day's evidence to the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket checks: Can learners state at least one observation with a number or day (e.g. 'maize 88, beans 80', 'maize emerged Day 7')? Can they link it to the driving question? Quick oral probing during the gallery walk: 'What is one thing your model cannot yet explain?' Record learners who cannot yet distinguish observation from explanation for follow-up in Lesson 2. Keep the models and exit tickets for revision at the end of the unit.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson ask yourself: Did every learner, including quiet ones, draw an initial model and post at least one idea? Which baseline ideas (e.g. 'all healthy seeds germinate', 'growth is just height') were most common, and how will I address them without giving answers too early? Were the questions on the DQB mostly about causes, and did they include the growth, branching and germination ideas we need? Did the video or sketch strips work with the available power and internet? How well did the learners use simple, clear scientific English for germination, emergence and growth, and which terms do I need to reinforce in Lesson 2? What will I change to make sure larger groups and shared materials still allow everyone to participate?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Maize H614 and bean Rosecoco were planted on the same day at Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale. The bean radicle came out on Day 3 and emerged on Day 8; maize radicle on Day 4 and emerged on Day 7. By Day 14, 88 of 100 maize and 80 of 100 bean seeds had germinated, so 12 and 20 did not, even though some looked healthy. Maize was taller from Day 14 onward, stems thickened, and the bean branched by Day 25.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The two crops behave differently even with the same rain and planting day. Germination (radicle comes out) and emergence (shoot appears above soil) are not the same event. Growth is not only getting taller: stems also thicken and plants branch. We have many questions, such as what growth and development mean and why healthy-looking seeds do not germinate.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Our first ideas are only tentative: we think the differences may be due to the seeds, the soil, water, age or pests, but we do not yet have evidence. Our initial models and DQB questions are our baseline, and we will revise them as we collect evidence. The next question is: What is growth and development?

LESSONS.title: Growth vs Development and Inside the Seed: Maize H614 and Rosecoco Beans
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (single lesson; if double period available, extend the Observe Phase)
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: growth, development, monocot, dicot, testa, micropyle, hilum, cotyledon, scutellum, endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza, plumule, radicle, epigeal, hypogeal

slo.purpose: Learners distinguish between growth and development and relate the structures of monocot (maize H614) and dicot (bean Rosecoco) seeds to their functions, so they can begin to explain why Mr. Wafula's two crops behaved differently.
slo.knowledge: a) Distinguish between growth and development in living organisms. b) Relate structures of monocot and dicot seeds to their functions. Growth = permanent, irreversible increase in size/dry mass (e.g. maize stem width 6 to 14 to 22 mm; bean height 4 cm at Day 7 to 44 cm at Day 42). Development = changes in complexity and form through differentiation (e.g. radicle to roots, unifoliate to trifoliate leaves, branching). Bean (dicot): testa, micropyle, hilum, two cotyledons storing food, plumule, radicle. Maize (monocot): fruit/seed coat fused, one cotyledon (scutellum), endosperm food store, coleoptile protecting plumule, coleorhiza protecting radicle.
slo.skills: Observing, drawing and labelling seed specimens (NGSS SEP: Developing and Using Models); asking questions; analysing data (heights and stem widths) to classify changes as growth or development; constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning; communicating in simple, clear scientific English.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity and care when handling living material; Unity: works harmoniously with group members when sharing seed specimens and hand lenses; respect for peers' ideas during Think-Pair-Share and the Gallery Walk. Learning to Learn: reflects on own Day 1 drawing and adjusts it.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Lesson 2 focus: What do we mean by growth and development, and how are the maize and bean seeds built to support them?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 launched the phenomenon (Mr. Wafula's maize H614 and Rosecoco beans, planted on the same day, behaving differently) and posted the DQB question 'What is growth and development?'. This lesson answers that question and gives the seed-structure vocabulary and ideas needed to later explain dormancy and germination. It ends by raising the next question: What is seed dormancy? Why can a healthy-looking seed with a testa and an embryo fail to germinate?
slo.safetyNotes: Soak seeds overnight so they can be cut safely. Use a blunt knife or razor blade only under teacher control (teacher or one trained learner per group cuts the seed, away from the body). Do not taste seeds; some may be treated with pesticide (e.g. the purple or pink dressing on commercial seed). Wash hands after handling seeds. Keep specimens on trays or paper; wipe up spilled water to prevent slipping.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng's Form 3 class returns to Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale. From the Lesson 1 time-lapse, the class saw maize H614 and Rosecoco beans planted on the same day with the same 25 mm rain, yet they emerged on different days (maize Day 7, beans Day 8) and grew differently. The DQB question 'What is growth and development?' now needs an answer. Learners first predict which of several changes are growth and which are development, then observe and draw soaked maize and bean seeds (using readily available seeds, hand lenses and a blunt blade, in groups of 4 to 5), and use the Day 14 stem width and height numbers as examples of growth. They explain what each seed part does, apply it to how each seed becomes a seedling (without teaching dormancy or germination conditions, which come in Lessons 3 and 4), update the DQB and revise their Day 1 model. The lesson ends with a new question: What is seed dormancy?

framework.learnerExperience: Wanjiru's DQB question is read aloud: 'What is growth and development?'. Learners individually write a one-sentence prediction for each of 6 changes from Mr. Wafula's field: (1) bean shoot height rising from 4 cm at Day 7 to 44 cm at Day 42; (2) maize stem width rising from 6 mm (Day 14) to 22 mm (Day 42); (3) bean getting first unifoliate leaves on Day 12 and trifoliate leaves on Day 18; (4) bean branching by Day 25; (5) a maize seed swelling after the 25 mm rain; (6) the radicle emerging on Day 3 (bean) and Day 4 (maize). For each they write G (growth), D (development) or Both and a reason. They then predict, by quick sketch, what is inside a maize grain and a bean seed. Think-Pair-Share: think alone 2 minutes, pair for 2 minutes, share.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the 6 changes on the board or on a prepared chart (no electricity needed). Say: 'Look at what Mr. Wafula saw in his field. Which of these is just getting bigger, and which is getting more complex or changing form? Write your own idea first.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds of silence after the question; do not rescue. Circulate and note ideas. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers): 'Tell us your G, D or Both for number 3, and why.' Record learners' words verbatim on a Predict column on the board, and do NOT confirm correct answers yet. Say: 'Hold on to your predictions; we will test them with evidence.' Ask: 'What do you think is inside this seed that lets it become a plant?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share, with Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) as the frame: committing to a prediction first exposes learners' everyday meaning of 'growth' (just getting taller) so that evidence in the Observe and Explain phases can confront it. Pair talk builds understanding by forcing learners to justify their ideas in simple scientific English before hearing the class.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: learners write a reason (not just a letter) for at least 4 of 6 items; at least 4 cold-called pairs give a reason using words like 'bigger', 'thicker', 'changes shape' or 'new part'. Probing to detect misconceptions: 'Is growth only getting taller?' 'Does swelling of a seed in water count as growth?' Tally on the board how many pairs predict each item as G, D or Both. Teacher notes the misconception 'growth = height only' for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 to 5 (one set of specimens per group; share hand lenses between groups) receive soaked maize H614 grains, soaked Rosecoco bean seeds (soaked overnight) and a reading handout/textbook page on seed structure. (1) Observe the outside of each seed with a hand lens: bean testa, hilum (scar), micropyle (tiny pore); maize grain surface with the scar and the darker area marking the embryo. (2) Under teacher guidance, one learner removes the bean testa and splits the bean into two cotyledons, finding the plumule and radicle. The maize grain is cut lengthwise along the flat side to show the scutellum (one cotyledon), endosperm, coleoptile covering the plumule and coleorhiza covering the radicle. (3) Draw and label both seeds in their notebooks (size at least half a page, pencil, ruled label lines, title and magnification note). (4) Complete a table: Part | Where found (bean/maize) | Function (e.g. testa protects the seed; micropyle lets water in; hilum is the scar where seed was attached; cotyledons store food in the bean; scutellum absorbs food from the endosperm for the maize embryo; endosperm stores food; coleoptile protects the plumule; coleorhiza protects the radicle; plumule becomes shoot; radicle becomes root). (5) Use the given measurements as growth examples: Day 14 to Day 42 stem width (maize 6, 14, 22 mm; bean 2, 4, 6 mm) and shoot height Day 7 to 42 (maize 3 to 125 cm; bean 4 to 44 cm). Learners calculate the increase in stem width (maize +16 mm, bean +4 mm).
framework.teacherMoves: Before the lesson, soak the seeds overnight; if seeds are scarce, provide 1 set per group or use photographs/teacher-drawn charts. Model safe cutting: 'I cut away from my body, on the tray, and only the cutter handles the blade.' Circulate with the observation checklist. Ask: 'What do you see at the end of the bean where it was attached to the pod? What is the tiny hole next to it for?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each probe. Ask: 'Where would the bean's food be stored? How is that different from maize?' Cold-call 3 groups to hold up their cut seeds and name one visible structure. If a group lacks specimens, hand over a teacher-prepared labelled drawing for them to annotate. Clarify difficult words (testa = seed coat, cotyledon = seed leaf, scutellum = shield-like cotyledon of maize) and write them on the board with simple meanings. If an internet-free class cannot play the time-lapse videos, recall the Day 7 maize and Day 8 bean emergence events from the Lesson 1 table.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Observe step): direct observation of the real seeds and the growth data provides the evidence that learners compare with their earlier predictions. Drawing and labelling is a Developing and Using Models practice: it makes structures visible and links each part to a job (structure-function), which is the foundation for explaining why maize and beans emerge differently.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist (tick/cross): (a) correctly identifies testa, micropyle, hilum on the bean; (b) separates cotyledons and finds plumule and radicle; (c) identifies the scutellum, endosperm and coleoptile in maize; (d) drawing is large, has title, label lines that do not cross, and correct proportions; (e) all members take part in handling and discussing. Expect at least 80% of groups to label at least 6 parts correctly. Oral probe: 'Which part would protect the shoot tip as it pushes through soil in maize?' (coleoptile). Misconceptions to catch: 'maize has no cotyledon' or 'the endosperm is the embryo'.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the predictions from the Predict Phase and write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) statement in their notebooks: Claim: which of the 6 changes are growth and which are development. Evidence: the numbers (e.g. maize stem width 6 mm at Day 14 to 22 mm at Day 42; bean height 4 cm at Day 7 to 44 cm at Day 42; bean's leaf types changing from unifoliate on Day 12 to trifoliate on Day 18; branching by Day 25) and what they saw in the seeds. Reasoning: growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size or dry mass (so a seed only swelling with water is not true growth, because water can be lost again), while development is increasing complexity and form through cell differentiation (radicle becoming root, plumule becoming shoot with leaves, branching). They then use the seed structure to explain: 'Both seeds have an embryo with a radicle and plumule, but the bean stores food in two large cotyledons and the maize in an endosperm absorbed by one scutellum.' They tie this to what they saw in Lesson 1: maize pushes up a coleoptile (Day 7) while the bean pushes up an arched hypocotyl and lifts its cotyledons (Day 8). In pairs, they state one way the seed structure may help explain a difference in emergence.
framework.teacherMoves: Ask: 'Which of the 6 changes belongs in the growth box, which in the development box, and which in both? What is your evidence?' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 5 learners in different groups, each for a different item. Press for reasoning: 'How do you know it is permanent? Could the swelling be reversed if the seed dried?' Introduce the conventions: 'germination is the radicle emerging; emergence is the shoot appearing above the soil.' Use sentence starters on the board: 'I claim ... because the data show ... which means ...'. Address the misconception 'growth = taller only' using the stem width data: 'Maize widened by 16 mm and the bean by 4 mm. Is that growth if the plant did not get taller? Yes: size increased.' Do NOT teach dormancy or germination conditions; if a learner asks why some healthy seeds did not germinate, say: 'Great question. Hold on to it; we will see what the seed structure tells us in the next lesson. Put it on the DQB.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): learners must link a claim (growth or development) to specific data and to a scientific definition, which deepens understanding beyond memorising definitions. Discussion and questioning connects the seed structure to the DQB question about how maize and beans behave differently.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check CER notebooks: strong response contains a clear claim, at least 2 numbers as evidence (such as 6 to 22 mm, or 4 to 44 cm) and reasoning using 'permanent, irreversible increase' or 'differentiation / change in form'. Look for: at least 70% of learners correctly classify the stem width as growth and branching or leaf type change as development. Peer review: swap notebooks with a partner and underline the evidence in green and the reasoning in blue. Oral probe: 'Why can't we say a dry seed swelling in water is growth?' Record misconceptions on the board.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners go to the class DQB (a chart or wall space). They (1) find Wanjiru's question 'What is growth and development?' and, in groups, write an evidence-based answer on a sticky note/paper strip (e.g. 'Growth is a permanent increase in size such as maize stem width 6 to 22 mm; development is a change in form such as bean leaves changing from unifoliate to trifoliate') and place it beside the question. (2) Write new questions raised by the seed observation (e.g. 'Why do some healthy-looking bean seeds with a complete embryo not germinate?', 'Does the testa stop water entering?', 'Why does the maize leave its scutellum underground?'). (3) Link the DQB to the driving question: 'How does this lesson help explain the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and beans?' The key new question that the class agrees to investigate next: What is seed dormancy?
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Choose one thing you now understand and one thing that still puzzles you. Write each on its own strip.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds before groups begin writing. Cold-call 3 groups to read their strip aloud and say where it should go on the board (answered, partly answered, new). Model sorting by pinning Wanjiru's question as 'answered in part: definitions and seed parts known'. Highlight the strips that ask about healthy seeds failing: 'These strips connect to the testa and embryo we just saw. We will investigate them in the next lesson: What is seed dormancy?' Keep a copy of the DQB in the teacher's notebook in case the chart is removed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the Driving Question Board: the DQB makes the class's growing understanding visible, shows learners how this lesson's evidence (definitions, seed structure) fits into the larger puzzle, and lets their own questions drive the next investigation, which builds ownership.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: every group posts at least one answer strip and one new question; at least 2 questions refer to the testa, embryo or healthy seeds failing to germinate; answers use the terms growth/development correctly with an example from Mr. Wafula's field. Oral probe: 'Which of our questions was answered today and what was the evidence?' Note learners who post only vocabulary questions (what is a hilum?) and prompt them toward 'why' or 'how' questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 (Lesson 1) drawing/model of how Mr. Wafula's maize and beans grow. Working individually for 5 minutes, they revise it using a different colour pen: (1) add labelled cross-section drawings of the maize H614 grain and Rosecoco bean seed inside the soil, showing the embryo parts (radicle, plumule), food stores (cotyledons in bean; endosperm and scutellum in maize) and protective parts (testa; coleoptile and coleorhiza); (2) add arrows showing that radicle becomes root and plumule becomes shoot; (3) add a small box with the definitions of growth and development and one example of each from the field data; (4) add a question mark where the model still cannot explain why some healthy-looking seeds did not germinate. In a short Gallery Walk (3 minutes), groups display their revised models, and visitors leave one 'star' (what is good) and one 'wish' (what to improve). The lesson closes with an exit ticket.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Use a new colour so we can see how your thinking has changed since Day 1.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds, then circulate. Ask individuals: 'Which part of your model is new today? What evidence led you to add it?' Cold-call 3 learners to explain one revision. During the Gallery Walk, instruct: 'Walk clockwise, spend 30 seconds at each model, leave one star and one wish.' Collect exit tickets: (1) 'What evidence did we gather today?' (2) 'How does this help answer our driving question about maize and beans?' (3) 'One question I still have.' Close with: 'Next time we ask: What is seed dormancy? Why would a seed that looks healthy not germinate?' Homework: bring one dry bean and one maize grain from home or the market and note differences in the outside appearance of the testa.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision with a Gallery Walk: revising the Day 1 model with evidence from this lesson shows how understanding changes, and peer review sharpens scientific communication. The question mark in the model keeps the gap (healthy seeds not germinating) visible, setting up Lesson 3.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check: look for at least 3 new labelled structures, correct direction of arrows (radicle to root, plumule to shoot), definitions with an example, and a question mark gap. Exit ticket success criteria: names at least 2 pieces of evidence (seed observations and a growth number such as 6 to 22 mm) and links them to the driving question. Peer review: stars and wishes refer to specific parts of the model. Quick quiz option (2 questions): 'Name the part of maize that protects the shoot tip.' 'Give one example of growth and one of development from the bean.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: 1) Did learners move beyond 'growth = getting taller' by using the stem width data? Which examples convinced them? 2) How many groups correctly identified the scutellum, endosperm and coleoptile in maize; did sharing specimens or hand lenses slow groups down? 3) Which seed-structure terms needed the most clarification in simple English? 4) Did the CER writing show evidence plus reasoning, or just definitions? 5) Which questions on the DQB reveal curiosity about dormancy, so that Lesson 3 can start from the learners' own words? 6) If electricity or the time-lapse videos were unavailable, did the teacher-prepared alternatives (charts and the Lesson 1 events table) work? What would you change next time?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed soaked Rosecoco bean seeds (testa, hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons, plumule, radicle) and maize H614 grains (one cotyledon called the scutellum, endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza, plumule, radicle). We also used Mr. Wafula's data: maize stem width 6, 14, 22 mm and shoot height 3 to 125 cm; bean stem width 2, 4, 6 mm and shoot height 4 to 44 cm.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size or dry mass; development is a change in complexity and form through differentiation. Monocot (maize) and dicot (bean) seeds have different structures: the bean stores food in two cotyledons, while the maize stores food in the endosperm and one cotyledon (scutellum) absorbs it. Each part has a function, such as protection, food storage, and forming the root and shoot.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Maize and beans differ in seed structure, which is part of why they emerge differently (maize by a coleoptile on Day 7; bean by an arched hypocotyl lifting two cotyledons on Day 8). Both seeds contain an embryo and a testa or coat, but the structure alone does not yet explain why some healthy-looking seeds did not germinate. This raises the next question: What is seed dormancy?

LESSONS.title: Seed Dormancy: Why Do Healthy-Looking Seeds Not Germinate?
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one single period; Part B scarification and soaking set-up runs in the same period, with germination checked in Lesson 4 or as a take-home observation)
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: seed dormancy, viable, non-viable, testa, impermeable seed coat, scarification, soaking, embryo, abscisic acid, Rosecoco, H614, Mr. Wafula, Kitale

slo.purpose: Learners use seed specimens and a simple scarification investigation to explain why 8 healthy-looking Rosecoco bean seeds on Mr. Wafula's farm did not germinate, and how dormancy can be broken. This moves the class from the puzzle of healthy-looking seeds toward the next question: how does germination occur?
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to: (1) define dormancy as a viable seed failing to germinate even in favourable conditions; (2) distinguish dormant-but-viable seeds from non-viable seeds and from seeds lost to pests or waterlogging, using the 12 non-germinating maize and 20 non-germinating bean seeds; (3) outline causes of dormancy (hard impermeable seed coat, immature embryo, chemical inhibitors such as abscisic acid); (4) outline ways of breaking dormancy (scarification, soaking, and others) and relate them to the cause; (5) explain the significance of dormancy to the plant and to the farmer.
slo.skills: Observing and examining seed specimens (hand lens, fingernail and water-uptake test); Planning and carrying out an investigation (NGSS SEP 3); Analysing and interpreting data (NGSS SEP 4): sorting the 12 and 20 non-germinating seeds into categories and computing the 7 of 8 result; Constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (NGSS SEP 6); Engaging in argument from evidence (NGSS SEP 7); Communicating in simple, clear scientific English.
slo.attitudes: Learning to Learn: the learner reflects on their own work and adjusts accordingly while carrying out activities to demonstrate ways of breaking seed dormancy. Unity: the learner works harmoniously with others in the group while examining specimens and setting up treatments. Curiosity and respect for evidence when a prediction turns out to be wrong.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? Lesson focus: Why did some healthy-looking bean seeds not germinate, and how can the farmer make them germinate? Pose to the class: 'If the rain, soil and planting day were the same, what is different about the seed itself?'
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 raised the puzzle of healthy-looking seeds that did not germinate at Mr. Wafula's farm. Lesson 2 gave learners the structure of the maize H614 and Rosecoco seeds, including the seed coat (testa) and embryo. Lesson 3 uses that structure to explain one cause: a hard, impermeable testa makes 8 viable bean seeds dormant (7 of 8 germinated after scarification). It also sorts the other failures (12 maize, 20 beans) into viable versus not viable. Remaining failures (waterlogging, lack of oxygen) lead to Lesson 4 and the new question: 'How does germination occur?'
slo.safetyNotes: Scarify seeds with sandpaper or a nail file, never with a razor blade or knife; rub away from fingers and hold seeds on a flat tray. Use only warm (not boiling) water for soaking; the teacher alone handles hot water for demonstration. Wash hands after handling seeds, as some stored seed may be treated with pesticide: label and keep any treated seed away from learners, use only untreated seed. Do not taste any seed. Keep seeds and water away from eyes. Clear spills to prevent slipping.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng's Form 3 class at a Kitale secondary school returns to Mr. Wafula's field: 100 maize H614 and 100 Rosecoco bean seeds were planted on the same day, 3 cm deep, after 25 mm of rain. At Day 14, 88 maize and 80 beans had germinated. Learners predict why 8 healthy-looking bean seeds sat in the soil, then examine bean and maize seeds, sort the 12 and 20 non-germinating seeds into causes, and compare untreated and scarified (nicked) seeds. They use the field result that 7 of the 8 hard-coated beans germinated by Day 7 after scarification. Learners write a CER explanation, add questions to the Driving Question Board, and revise their Day 1 model by adding dormancy as one reason seeds differ. Offline-friendly: no electricity or internet is needed; teacher-prepared printed photos and a written summary of the Khan Academy 'Seed dormancy' reading replace the online resource where there is no connectivity.

framework.learnerExperience: (8 minutes) Learners look at the data card: Day 14 results out of 100: maize 88 germinated, 12 did not; beans 80 germinated, 20 did not. Mr. Wafula dug up the failed seeds and found that 8 bean seeds looked healthy, firm and unspoiled. THINK (individually, 1 minute): 'Why might a healthy-looking Rosecoco bean seed refuse to germinate when the rain, soil, depth and planting day were the same?' Learners write a prediction and a reason in their notebooks. PAIR (2 minutes): compare predictions. SHARE (3 minutes): groups give predictions, e.g. 'the seed is old', 'no water got in', 'the seed is sleeping'. Teacher records predictions on the board under headings: seed problem / environment problem / not sure. They then predict: 'If we scratch the hard outside of the seed, will it germinate?' Each learner records Yes/No and why. This is a POE prediction to be tested later.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the data card on the board or as a printed handout (no electricity needed). Say: 'Mr. Wafula planted on the same day, in the same field, with the same rain. Eight healthy-looking bean seeds still did not germinate. What could be different about the seed itself?' Give the Think step 1 minute of silent writing. WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking for ideas before accepting any answer; count silently. Cold-call 4 learners from different groups (not only volunteers) with: 'Wanjiru, what did you and your partner predict?' Ask a follow-up probe: 'What makes you think so?' Do NOT correct predictions; write them all. Ask: 'Which of these ideas could we test today?' Point to the Day 1 model and the DQB question 'Why do healthy-looking seeds not germinate?'. Clarify the words 'viable' (alive embryo) and 'dormant' (viable seed that fails to germinate in favourable conditions) only after predictions are shared.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share inside Predict-Observe-Explain (POE). Individual thinking makes every learner commit to an idea before seeing evidence; pairing lets learners rehearse and refine wording in simple scientific English; the whole-class share surfaces a range of ideas (old seed, no water, pests) that later evidence will sort. Written predictions let learners see for themselves later if they changed their ideas.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probing and misconception check. Observable indicators: (a) learner writes a prediction with a reason, not only 'yes/no'; (b) at least 3 different ideas are recorded on the board; (c) listen for the misconception 'a seed that does not germinate is dead'; note names of learners who hold it and revisit in the Explain phase. Teacher tallies on a checklist how many learners predicted that scratching the seed would help (Yes/No).

framework.learnerExperience: (14 minutes) Part A: Examine seed specimens (6 minutes). Groups of 4-5 receive a tray with about 10 untreated Rosecoco bean seeds, 10 maize H614 seeds (or equivalents), a hand lens, sandpaper, and a cup of water. Groups: (1) observe the testa, hilum and micropyle with the hand lens; test the hardness by pressing with a fingernail; (2) soak 3 seeds untreated and 3 seeds scarified (rubbed on sandpaper until a small dull patch shows, taking care not to damage the embryo) in separate labelled cups of water; (3) record in a table: seed type, treatment, appearance, hardness. Part B: Sort the non-germinating seeds (5 minutes). Using the data card with the reasons for non-germination: Maize (12): 5 eaten or rotted by fungi/pests, 4 old stored seed with dead embryos (not viable), 3 planted in a waterlogged low patch (no oxygen). Beans (20): 8 hard impermeable seed coat (dormant, healthy-looking), 6 waterlogged low patch, 4 old seed with dead embryos, 2 eaten by pests. Learners complete a table with columns: cause, maize, beans, viable (alive embryo)? dormant? and check totals 12 and 20. Part C: Field result (3 minutes): After the 8 hard-coated bean seeds were scarified (nicked) and replanted, 7 germinated by Day 7. Learners write the fraction and the percentage (7 of 8 = 87.5%, about 88%) and note what the 1 remaining seed might mean. Learners who finish early read the printed Khan Academy 'Seed dormancy' summary card (teacher-prepared, offline) and list two causes of dormancy.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the period, prepare trays and sandpaper, with beans from the local market (e.g. Kitale or Nairobi) soaked or dry as needed. Circulate and say: 'Show me where water could enter this seed. What does the testa feel like?' and 'Fatuma, what is your group seeing under the hand lens?' Remind: 'Rub gently, away from your fingers, only until the shiny surface turns dull.' Check group roles (reader, recorder, handler, reporter) to maintain Unity. Use WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question, e.g. 'Which of these seeds could still grow if the conditions were right?' Cold-call 3 groups to report their sorting of the beans and 2 groups for maize. Probe: 'Is a non-viable seed the same as a dormant seed? How do you know?' Use the printed copy of the table to direct learners to compare maize (0 dormant) with beans (8 dormant). Without electricity, use drawings on the board in place of video. If digital resources work, show the Khan Academy seed dormancy page or the bean time-lapse. Clarify difficult terms (impermeable, viable, scarification) on the board in simple English.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain: the Observe step provides evidence that directly tests the predictions (does scratching the testa change water uptake and germination?). Sorting data into categories (dormant, non-viable, pests, waterlogged) helps learners see that 'not germinating' has several different causes, only one of which is dormancy. Comparing maize (0 dormant) and beans (8 dormant) links back to the seed structure learned in Lesson 2 (testa and embryo).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist during the practical (tick when seen): handles seeds safely and scarifies gently; labels cups correctly; records observations in a table; notices that the scarified seeds take up water or show a swollen look sooner than untreated ones; sums 5+4+3 = 12 and 8+6+4+2 = 20 correctly; correctly identifies 8 as the dormant group. Peer check: partners swap tables and check totals. Oral probe: 'Which of the 20 non-germinating beans still had a living embryo?' (Expected: the 8 dormant and the 6 waterlogged seeds could be viable; the 4 old seeds were dead.) Flag learners who place the dormant seeds under 'dead'.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 minutes) Learners build a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) explanation in their groups for the question: 'Why did 8 healthy-looking Rosecoco bean seeds not germinate at Mr. Wafula's farm, and why did 7 of them germinate after scarification?' Sentence frames on the board: Claim: 'The 8 seeds did not germinate because ___.' Evidence: 'The data show ___ (for example 8 beans had a hard impermeable seed coat; 7 of 8 germinated by Day 7 after scarification; maize had 0 dormant seeds).' Reasoning: 'This means ___ because the testa ___ so water and oxygen ___ and the embryo ___.' Then learners connect to ways of breaking dormancy: scarification (nicking or rubbing the testa), soaking in water for some hours, plus others (exposure to cold or light, passing through animals' digestive tracts, fire or smoke, hormone treatment such as gibberellin). They match each cause to a way of breaking it (hard testa to scarification or soaking; chemical inhibitor such as abscisic acid to leaching with water, cold or gibberellin; immature embryo to after-ripening/storage). Significance of dormancy: seeds survive dry or cold seasons and germinate when the rains come, spreading germination over time; the farmer uses scarification to get a uniform stand. Learners revise their Part 1 prediction: 'Was I right? What did the evidence change?' Then Think-Pair-Share: 'Does dormancy explain ALL the failures in the field? Which failures still need explaining?' (Expected: waterlogging, pests and dead seed; waterlogging and oxygen lead to Lesson 4.)
framework.teacherMoves: Model one CER sentence set, then let groups write. Say: 'Your claim must answer the question. Your evidence must be a number or an observation. Your reasoning must say why.' Circulate and check that each group cites the numbers 8, 7 of 8 and 0 dormant maize. WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone, and cold-call 4 groups to read claims, then 3 learners to challenge: 'Kiprop, do you agree with their reasoning? What evidence supports or weakens it?' Probe: 'If the testa is hard, how could the seed ever germinate in a natural field?' (Expected: weathering, microbes, animals, soil abrasion, fire.) Ask: 'Why might dormancy be useful for a wild plant but a problem for Mr. Wafula?' Correct the misconception that dormant seeds are dead or diseased. Confirm vocabulary: dormancy, viable, scarification. Do not teach germination conditions (water, oxygen, temperature) or the types of germination; say: 'That belongs to our next lesson.' Clarify the hormone idea only briefly: 'Abscisic acid helps keep seeds dormant; we meet hormones fully in Lesson 7.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) turns the observations and field numbers into a causal explanation, forcing learners to link data (8 dormant, 7 of 8 germinating after scarification, 0 dormant maize) to the mechanism (impermeable testa blocking water and oxygen entry). Peer challenge and Think-Pair-Share strengthen argument from evidence. Matching cause to remedy shows that the way of breaking dormancy depends on why the seed is dormant.
framework.formativeAssessment: Score each group CER on a 3-point rubric: Claim (answers the question), Evidence (cites at least 2 numbers from the data), Reasoning (links the hard testa to blocked water or oxygen uptake and to the effect of scarification). Observable indicators: uses the word 'viable' correctly; separates dormancy from death, pests and waterlogging; matches at least 3 of 4 causes to ways of breaking dormancy. Quick quiz (2 minutes, oral or on slips): 'Name two ways to break dormancy.' 'Is a dormant seed alive?' Peer review: one group exchanges its CER with another and gives one star and one wish.

framework.learnerExperience: (4 minutes) Learners return to the Driving Question Board started in Lesson 1 (chart paper or a wall space with sticky notes). Wanjiru's earlier question 'Why do healthy-looking seeds not germinate?' is moved into the 'Partly answered' column with a note: 'Dormancy (hard testa) explained 8 of 20 bean failures. 7 of 8 germinated after scarification.' Learners add new questions on sticky notes, e.g. 'How does germination occur?', 'Why did the 6 beans in the waterlogged patch fail?', 'What does a seed need to germinate?', 'Does maize ever have dormancy?', 'Why did the last 1 of 8 seeds not germinate?' Each group posts at least one question and says which lesson might answer it. Individually, learners complete an exit ticket: (1) 'What evidence did we gather today?' (2) 'How does this help answer our driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Which question from our board did we answer today, and which new question did the evidence raise?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking suggestions. Cold-call 3 learners to read a new question and where to place it. Highlight the question that leads to the next lesson: 'How does germination occur?' Sort questions: answered, partly answered, new. Say: 'Wanjiru started this question in Lesson 1, so what can we now tell her?' Collect exit tickets at the door. Read a sample at the end of the day to see who still thinks dormant seeds are dead.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the Driving Question Board: placing evidence next to questions helps learners track how each lesson contributes to the driving question, and turns gaps in understanding (e.g. waterlogging, oxygen, germination process) into the purpose for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket check: each learner states at least one piece of evidence with a number (e.g. 8 dormant beans or 7 of 8 germinated) and links it to differences between seeds, not to rain or planting date. Observable indicators: at least one new, testable question per group; questions posted in the right column; learners can say whether a question is answered, partly answered or new. Teacher notes the number of exit tickets that correctly separate dormant from non-viable seeds.

framework.learnerExperience: (4 minutes) Learners take out their Day 1 drawing and explanation of why Mr. Wafula's maize and beans behaved differently. Using a different coloured pen, each learner revises the model by: (1) adding a labelled seed drawing of a bean with an intact, hard testa that blocks water entry (label testa, embryo, hilum, micropyle); (2) adding a box 'Dormant but viable: 8 beans, 0 maize' with an arrow 'scarification, 7 of 8 germinated by Day 7'; (3) adding a box 'Not germinated for other reasons: dead embryo, pests, waterlogging'; (4) writing one sentence: 'Seeds differ because of seed condition (dormancy, viability) as well as the environment.' They mark with a question mark what the model still cannot explain (how the seed actually starts to germinate, and why waterlogging stops germination). A few learners pin their revised drawings for a short Gallery Walk next lesson. Home task: soak 5 untreated and 5 scarified bean seeds (or use leftover seeds) in cups at home and record the water uptake after 24 hours in the notebook.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Day 1 model. Use a new colour so we can see how your thinking has changed.' Circulate and prompt: 'Where in your model does the testa appear? What happens to the 8 seeds in your drawing?' Insist on correct labels (testa, embryo, cotyledon) from Lesson 2. WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before asking, 'What is still missing from your model?' Cold-call 3 learners to share one revision and one remaining question. Remind learners not to add the conditions of germination yet, as we will do that after the next lesson. Set the home task and safety reminder (use only untreated seeds; wash hands). Ask learners to bring a clean plastic cup or jar for Lesson 4.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: learners update the Day 1 drawing with new evidence, which makes visible the change in their thinking and ties dormancy to the anchoring phenomenon. Marking the unanswered parts with question marks keeps the model as a tool for the next lesson's inquiry. A short Gallery Walk (in the next lesson or at the end of this one if time permits) provides peer review.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check using three criteria: (1) includes dormancy with a correct cause (hard impermeable testa) and the numbers 8 and 7 of 8; (2) separates dormant from non-viable seeds and from pests or waterlogging; (3) identifies at least one unanswered question. Peer review: partners tick the criteria and give one suggestion. Observable indicator: revisions in the second colour show a real change, not just a copy of the old drawing.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: (1) Did learners separate dormant seeds from dead seeds, or did many still say 'a seed that does not germinate is dead'? Which evidence changed their minds (the 7 of 8 result, the water-uptake test)? (2) Were the groups able to scarify safely and with limited sandpaper and trays, and how could sharing materials in a large class improve? (3) Did the CER explanations include numbers (8, 7 of 8, 0 maize) and the link to a blocked testa, or only general statements? (4) Did the offline printed cards work well for learners without access to the Khan Academy page or videos? (5) Which new DQB questions came up (germination, oxygen, waterlogging), and do they match Lesson 4? (6) Which learners need support with terms such as viable, impermeable and scarification? Plan to revisit these with a short word wall, and check the home soaking results at the start of the next lesson.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What we observed: Bean seed testa is hard; scarified seeds took up water faster than untreated ones. In Mr. Wafula's field at Day 14, 12 maize (5 pests/rot, 4 dead embryos, 3 waterlogged) and 20 beans (8 hard seed coat, 6 waterlogged, 4 dead embryos, 2 pests) did not germinate. 8 dormant beans looked healthy; 7 of the 8 germinated by Day 7 after scarification.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What we learned: Dormancy is when a viable (living) seed fails to germinate even in favourable conditions. Causes include a hard impermeable testa, chemical inhibitors such as abscisic acid, and an immature embryo. Dormancy can be broken by scarification, soaking and other methods that match the cause. Dormancy helps wild seeds survive bad seasons but can delay germination on a farm. Not every failed seed is dormant: some are non-viable, eaten by pests or waterlogged.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How this helps explain the driving question: Some healthy-looking bean seeds did not germinate because of a hard, impermeable testa (dormancy), while no maize seeds were dormant. So differences in germination depend on the seed's structure and condition as well as the environment, not on the rain or planting date. Other failures (waterlogging, lack of oxygen) still need to be explained, which raises our next question: How does germination occur?

LESSONS.title: Germination: Conditions Necessary and Types (Hypogeal vs Epigeal) in Maize H614 and Rosecoco Beans
LESSONS.duration: 80 minutes (double period); jars set up earlier in the week so Day 5 results are ready
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: germination, emergence, water, oxygen, temperature, viable, hypogeal, epigeal, cotyledon, scutellum, hypocotyl, coleoptile, waterlogging, Predict-Observe-Explain, Claim-Evidence-Reasoning

slo.purpose: Learners use germination jars and time-lapse evidence to explain which conditions are necessary for germination (water, oxygen, suitable temperature) and how hypogeal (maize H614) and epigeal (bean Rosecoco) germination differ, so they can explain why some of Mr. Wafula's seeds failed and why the two crops emerged on different days.
slo.knowledge: Learners should be able to: (d) investigate conditions necessary for seed germination, and (e) investigate types of germination in plants. They will state that a viable, non-dormant seed needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate. They will distinguish germination (radicle emerges and the embryo resumes growth) from emergence (shoot appears above the soil). They will describe hypogeal germination (maize: scutellum stays underground, coleoptile pierces the soil, emergence Day 7) and epigeal germination (bean: hypocotyl arch lifts the cotyledons above ground, emergence Day 8).
slo.skills: Predicting from prior knowledge (POE); planning and carrying out a fair-test investigation with controlled variables; observing and recording data in a table; analysing and interpreting data (Day 5 jar counts); constructing evidence-based explanations (CER); using models and drawings to illustrate germination types; communicating in clear scientific English; collaborating in small groups with shared materials.
slo.attitudes: Core competency, Learning to Learn: the learner reflects on their own work and adjusts accordingly. Value, Unity: the learner works harmoniously with others while carrying out experiments to investigate conditions necessary for seed germination. Curiosity and respect for evidence, even when it contradicts a prediction.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? (Lesson 4 focus: What must be present for a seed to start growing, and how do maize and beans emerge differently?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 2 gave us the seed parts and Lesson 3 showed that a hard seed coat explains the healthy-looking bean seeds that did not germinate (dormancy). Now we test the remaining causes of failure for viable, non-dormant seeds: water, oxygen and temperature. We also explain why maize (emergence Day 7) and beans (emergence Day 8) appear differently even though both were planted on Day 0. This closes the germination part of the puzzle and raises the next question: How do plants show growth once they have emerged?
slo.safetyNotes: Use only clean seeds from the school store. Do not use treated (pesticide-coated) seed; wash hands after handling seeds and soil. Seeds dressed with chemicals are not to be put near the mouth. Wipe up spilled water to avoid slipping. Use cooled boiled water (not hot water) for the no-air jar. If a fridge is not available, use a cool clay pot with wet sand as an alternative. Sharing equipment: one jar set per group of 5-6 learners.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng's class (Form 3, Kitale) returns to Mr. Wafula's puzzle: 88 of 100 maize and 80 of 100 bean seeds germinated by Day 14. Lesson 3 explained 8 bean seeds as dormant, but other seeds failed for different reasons, including 6 beans and 3 maize in the waterlogged low patch. Learners predict what a seed needs, then examine the Day 5 results from Fatuma's germination jars (20 Rosecoco bean seeds per jar): water + air + 25 C = 18 germinated; dry = 0; no air = 1; cold (4 C) = 0. They use CER to claim which conditions are necessary and link the no-air jar to the waterlogged patch. In the second half, learners watch the time-lapse videos (or use teacher-prepared drawings/flip-cards if there is no electricity), compare maize (hypogeal, emergence Day 7) and bean (epigeal, emergence Day 8), and build labelled drawings. A Gallery Walk, DQB update and Day 1 model revision close the lesson. Everything is done in small groups with local materials: maize, beans, jars, cotton wool or cloth, sand, cooking oil.

framework.learnerExperience: (12 min) Learners recall Mr. Wafula's field: 25 mm of rain, same day, same field, yet 12 maize and 20 bean seeds did not germinate. Individually they write in their notebooks: (1) What does a healthy, non-dormant seed need to germinate? (2) Four jars, each with 20 Rosecoco beans, were set up: A) water + air + 25 C, B) dry, C) submerged in boiled cooled water with an oil layer (no air), D) wet but kept at 4 C. Predict how many seeds in each jar will germinate by Day 5 and give a reason. They then think-pair-share and record their predictions on the group chart. Next they predict how the maize and bean shoots will reach the surface: 'Will they emerge the same way?' and sketch their prediction.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the 4 jar set-up on the board or hold up the actual jars. Say: 'Mr. Wafula's seeds all got the same rain. Lesson 3 told us 8 beans were dormant. What else could stop a healthy seed from germinating?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds in silence before anyone speaks. Say: 'Write your own prediction first, no talking.' Give 2 minutes for individual writing, then 3 minutes for pairs. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers): 'Pair 3, what number did you predict for the dry jar, and why?' Record all predictions on the board without evaluating them. Ask: 'Who predicted something different from their partner? What was the disagreement?' Circulate and note misconceptions such as 'seeds need light to germinate' or 'soil is needed'. Do NOT correct them yet; say: 'We will let the jars tell us.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (POE) and Think-Pair-Share: Writing predictions before seeing evidence commits learners to a position, so surprises in the data (for example, that light and soil are not necessary) create cognitive conflict and drive deeper explanation. Think-Pair-Share gives every learner a voice in large classes and lets the teacher hear the range of ideas without calling on only the confident few.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: Does the learner write a numeric prediction for each jar? Does the reason mention water, air or warmth? Oral probing: 'Why do you think the dry jar will have no germination?' Note misconceptions (light needed, soil needed, all seeds will germinate regardless) on a class tally. Indicator of readiness: at least 3 of 4 predictions have a stated reason.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A (15 min): Groups (5-6) examine the prepared jars from Fatuma's set-up (20 Rosecoco seeds each, Day 5): Jar 1 water + air + 25 C; Jar 2 dry; Jar 3 no air (boiled cooled water with oil layer); Jar 4 cold (4 C). They count germinated seeds (radicle visible), record in a table: Jar 1 = 18, Jar 2 = 0, Jar 3 = 1, Jar 4 = 0. They identify the variable changed in each jar and the variables kept the same (seed variety, number of seeds, time). They also compare the 18 germinated with the 2 that did not and suggest why (e.g., one dormant or non-viable seed). They discuss the waterlogged low patch where 6 beans and 3 maize failed. Part B (10 min): Learners watch the two time-lapse clips (Bean Time-Lapse 25 days soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse) or study teacher-prepared labelled drawing cards for Day 3, 7, 8, 10, 12 events. They record in a table: bean radicle Day 3, hypocotyl arch and cotyledons above ground Day 8, first unifoliate leaves Day 12; maize radicle Day 4, coleoptile pierces soil Day 7, first leaf Day 10, scutellum stays underground. If time permits, they uncover a few soaked seeds in sand trays to see where the cotyledons are.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the lesson, set up the jars 5 days earlier (prepare a back-up set of photographs or a class chart of the results in case of failure). Say: 'Count carefully. A seed has germinated only when the radicle has come out. Two people count, one records.' Circulate with the observation checklist; ask: 'Which variable did your group change? How do you know the other jars are a fair test?' and 'Why must the number of seeds be 20 in each jar?' WAIT TIME 10 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to report their counts and compare with the key (18, 0, 1, 0). If counts differ, ask: 'What might explain the difference?' For the time-lapse: pause at Day 7-8 and ask: 'Where are the seed leaves of the bean? Where is the maize seed leaf?' If there is no electricity, show the drawing cards and say: 'This card replaces the video; read the days carefully.' Clarify terms: germination, emergence, radicle, hypocotyl, coleoptile, scutellum. Insist that learners use correct vocabulary: 'Say germination when the radicle comes out, emergence when the shoot appears above the soil.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Observe step) with controlled variables: Comparing jars that differ in only one condition lets learners isolate cause and effect, which is the core of a fair test. Linking the no-air jar to the waterlogged patch connects the lab model to the field phenomenon. The time-lapse gives dynamic evidence of the process that a static diagram cannot show.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist indicators: counts germinated seeds correctly using the radicle criterion; records data in a table with units (seeds out of 20); names the changed variable in each jar; names at least two controlled variables; records the Day 7 and Day 8 emergence events correctly. Oral probe: 'Why did one seed germinate in the no-air jar?' (accept: a small amount of dissolved oxygen or residual air). Peer check: partners confirm each other's counts.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Part A (12 min): CER on conditions. Groups write: Claim: 'Germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature.' Evidence: Jar 1 = 18 of 20, Jar 2 (dry) = 0, Jar 3 (no air) = 1, Jar 4 (cold) = 0. Reasoning: water activates enzymes and softens the seed, oxygen is needed for aerobic respiration to release energy for embryo growth, and a suitable temperature (about 20-25 C) lets enzymes work. They then explain why the waterlogged low patch on Mr. Wafula's farm caused 3 maize and 6 bean seeds to fail: soil pores filled with water, no oxygen. They also state which of the failures in the farm data are NOT explained by these conditions (pests, non-viable embryos, dormancy).
