(4) Were allergies and materials managed safely and were enough local materials available for all groups? (5) Did group roles (Kiprop leading, Otieno measuring, Fatuma recording) include everyone? (6) What should be done to prepare for Lesson 9, including checking models and the DQB sort? Also plan for any learners who need support with percentage calculations or simple scientific English.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that hibiscus or Duranta cuttings treated with natural sources rooted better than cuttings in plain water: out of 30 cuttings, plain water 9 (30%), bulb onion 21 (70%), Aloe vera gel 24 (80%) and cinnamon powder 18 (60%).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that a fair test changes only one variable and keeps others the same, that percentages let us compare treatments, and that hormones such as auxin at the cut base help cuttings form roots, so hormones can be applied in a school tree nursery.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Aloe vera gel is the best treatment because 80% of its cuttings rooted compared with 30% in the control, and the only difference was the treatment. This shows hormones affect plant growth and development, which helps answer our driving question about why plants grow differently: seed structure, seed condition, environment and hormones all play a part.

LESSONS.title: Consolidating the Evidence and Building the Final Model: Why Did Mr. Wafula's Maize and Beans Behave So Differently?
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: consolidation, final model, claim-evidence-reasoning, Driving Question Board, germination, emergence, dormancy, viability, hypogeal, epigeal, sigmoid growth curve, apical dominance, auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise evidence from Lessons 1-8 into one final, evidence-based explanation of why maize H614 and Rosecoco beans, planted on the same day in the same field on Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale, differed in germination, emergence and growth. They finalise their cumulative model and review the Driving Question Board (DQB).
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, learners should be able to: (1) distinguish between growth and development using the maize and bean data; (2) relate the structures of the monocot (maize) and dicot (bean) seeds to their functions and to hypogeal and epigeal emergence; (3) outline causes of seed failure, including dormancy (a hard seed coat in 8 of 100 beans), non-viability, pests and waterlogging; (4) state the conditions necessary for germination (water, oxygen, suitable temperature); (5) explain primary growth, the lack of true secondary growth in maize, the sigmoid growth curves and the roles of hormones including apical dominance.
slo.skills: Constructing explanations using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER); developing and revising models; analysing and interpreting data (counts out of 100, heights in cm, stem width in mm); engaging in argument from evidence during a Gallery Walk; communicating in simple, clear scientific English.
slo.attitudes: Unity: work harmoniously with group members while consolidating evidence. Learning to Learn: reflect on their own Day 1 model and adjust it based on evidence. Appreciate that the differences come from seed structure, seed condition and environment, not from the rain or the planting date.
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1-8 each supplied one piece of evidence. Lesson 9 joins the pieces into a single explanation. Learners finalise the cumulative model, sort the DQB questions into answered and still open, and prepare for Lesson 10, where they present the explanation and plan seedling sharing and selling.
slo.safetyNotes: No new practical work is required. Keep the jars, cuttings and seedlings from earlier lessons on a bench away from walkways. Learners wash their hands after handling soil, seeds or aloe gel. Treated seeds are not to be handled. Keep movement orderly during the Gallery Walk.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng opens with the original puzzle: Mr. Wafula planted maize H614 and Rosecoco beans on the same day (Day 0), 3 cm deep, after 25 mm of rain, yet 88 of 100 maize but only 80 of 100 beans germinated by Day 14, the bean emerged on Day 8 and the maize on Day 7, and some healthy-looking seeds never germinated. Learners predict how many of the puzzles they can now explain. They then observe by sorting evidence cards and data tables from Lessons 1-8 (germination breakdowns, jar results, heights, stem width, root length, hormone data). In the Explain phase they build a CER explanation for each puzzle and test it in a Gallery Walk. The class reviews the DQB, moving each question to Answered, Partly answered or Still open. Finally learners finalise their model by revising their Day 1 drawing, using a different colour for each change. Think-Pair-Share, POE, CER, Gallery Walk, model revision and DQB questioning are all used. No electricity or internet is needed; the time-lapse events are provided on a printed table or a teacher-prepared flip chart.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take out their Day 1 drawing and explanation. They read the three puzzles on the board: (1) Why did 12 of 100 maize and 20 of 100 beans not germinate by Day 14, including healthy-looking seeds? (2) Why did the maize emerge on Day 7 and the bean on Day 8, with the bean lifting its seed leaves and the maize leaving its scutellum underground? (3) Why was the maize 125 cm and the bean only 44 cm by Day 42, and why did a bean branch only after its tip was removed? Learners think alone, then write a prediction on a sticky note or in their exercise book: 'Which of these can I now explain, and what is my best one-line reason for each?' They also predict: 'If I changed only the rain, would the differences disappear?' Then they pair with a neighbour and share (Think-Pair-Share).
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: 'Mr. Wafula planted on the same day, in the same field, with the same 25 mm of rain. If the rain and the date were the same, what else could explain the difference? Think silently for 1 minute and write down your idea.' WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after each question before taking any answer. Circulate and note two or three Day 1 ideas that were misconceptions, such as 'the beans did not get enough rain'. Cold-call 4 pairs, one at a time, using 'Wanjiru, what did your partner say?' to encourage listening. Do not confirm or correct yet. Record the main predictions on the board under the heading 'Our predictions before we consolidate'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share and Predict (the first step of Predict-Observe-Explain). Writing predictions before reviewing the evidence makes learners' current ideas visible, so the later comparison shows how much their thinking has changed. The pairing step lets learners practise explaining in simple scientific English before speaking to the class.
framework.formativeAssessment: Oral probing: listen for learners who attribute the differences to rain or planting date, or who think growth means only getting taller. Observation checklist: tick whether each learner writes a prediction for all three puzzles. Indicator of readiness: at least 4 of the 6 groups can name one factor that is not rain or planting date (for example seed structure, dormancy or waterlogging).

framework.learnerExperience: In groups of 5-6, each group gets a set of evidence cards covering lessons 1-8: Card A, germination counts at Day 14 (maize 88 of 100, beans 80 of 100) and the reasons for non-germination (maize 12: 5 eaten or rotted by fungi/pests, 4 old non-viable seed, 3 waterlogged; beans 20: 8 hard seed coat, 6 waterlogged, 4 non-viable, 2 pests); Card B, scarification of the 8 hard-coated beans (7 of 8 germinated by Day 7); Card C, jar results for 20 bean seeds at Day 5 (water + air + 25 C = 18; dry = 0; no air = 1; cold at 4 C = 0); Card D, time-lapse events (maize: radicle Day 4, emergence Day 7, first leaf Day 10, 3 leaves Day 17; bean: radicle Day 3, emergence Day 8, first true leaves Day 12, trifoliate leaves Day 18, branching by Day 25); Card E, heights at Days 7-42 (maize 3, 12, 30, 62, 98, 125 cm; bean 4, 9, 18, 30, 40, 44 cm), stem width at Days 14, 28 and 42 (maize 6, 14, 22 mm; bean 2, 4, 6 mm) and root length (maize 10, 25, 40 cm; bean 8, 18, 26 cm); Card F, hormone evidence (apical dominance: intact tip = 0 branches at Day 25, tip removed at Day 20 = 3 branches by Day 32; gibberellin-soaked seeds germinate sooner; abscisic acid maintains dormancy) and Card G, the cuttings results (water 9, onion extract 21, aloe 24, cinnamon 18 rooted out of 30). Each group sorts the cards under the three puzzles, and checks the sums (5+4+3=12 and 8+6+4+2=20). Fatuma's jars, Otieno's height table and Kiprop's cuttings data can be shown at the bench for learners to check against the cards. Each learner records in a table: 'What did we observe?' and 'Which puzzle does it help with?'
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: 'Your job is detective work. Place every card under the puzzle it helps to solve. Some cards help with more than one puzzle.' Distribute the card sets and printed time-lapse event tables (use the flip chart if the video cannot be shown, and play the Bean Time-Lapse 25 days soil cross section and Growing corn time lapse only where available). Circulate with probing questions: 'Which cards show that dormancy is not the same as death?' 'If the seed coat is the problem, why did 7 of 8 germinate after nicking?' 'Look at the stem width. Does the maize get thicker the same way as the bean?' WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call 3 groups to report one connection that they found between two cards. Correct any mistakes in the arithmetic. Make sure learners note that waterlogging affected both crops (3 maize and 6 bean seeds) because it limits oxygen.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain (the Observe step) with data sorting. Sorting cards under a puzzle requires learners to judge what each piece of evidence says, so they move from isolated lesson facts to a connected network of evidence. The checks on totals build habits of data accuracy.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: Did the group place Card B and Card C correctly (for example, scarification evidence under dormancy)? Did learners read the data using units (cm, mm, days)? Quick oral check: ask any learner 'Out of 100 beans, how many failed because of the hard seed coat?' (Answer: 8.) Look for the misconception that all 20 non-germinating beans were dead; the correct answer is that 8 were viable but dormant.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes three CER explanations, one for each puzzle. Claim: a one-sentence answer. Evidence: at least two data points from the cards. Reasoning: the biological idea that links the data to the claim, using correct terms. Example for puzzle 1: Claim: 'The seeds failed for different reasons, and the healthy-looking ones were dormant, not dead.' Evidence: '8 of 20 non-germinating beans had a hard seed coat, and 7 of those 8 germinated after scarification.' Reasoning: 'A hard impermeable testa stops water entering, so the viable embryo stays dormant even in favourable conditions; the other failures were pests, non-viable embryos and waterlogging, which removes oxygen.' Learners then hold a Gallery Walk: groups post CER sheets, seed structure drawings and growth curve sketches on the walls, and rotate every 3 minutes with sticky notes marked 'Strong evidence', 'Needs a reason' or 'Question'. They then return to their own sheet and improve it. The class also discusses: 'Why do we say the differences came from seed structure, seed condition and environment, and not the rain?'
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng models one CER using puzzle 2 on the board, thinking aloud: 'My claim is that maize emerges earlier because... what evidence do I have?' Then she says: 'Now write your own. Evidence must have a number and a unit.' Provide sentence starters: 'The data show that...', 'This happens because...'. During the Gallery Walk, instruct 'Read, do not talk, for the first minute; then leave a sticky note with a question or praise.' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds before calling on anyone. Cold-call 5 learners in total across groups with questions such as: 'Kiprop, which evidence is the strongest for your claim and why?' 'Fatuma, what is the role of oxygen in germination?' Press for reasoning: 'How do we know it was not the rain?' Clarify terms: germination (radicle emerges), emergence (shoot appears above the soil), growth (permanent irreversible increase in size) and development (changes in form or complexity). Make sure learners link the hypogeal (maize, scutellum stays underground) and epigeal (bean, cotyledons lifted) patterns to the structure of the seeds. For puzzle 3, make sure they discuss the maize growth: steepest between Day 21 and 35 (increases of 32 and 36 cm per week), slowing after Day 35 (27 cm); the bean steepest between Day 14 and 28 (9 and 12 cm per week) and flattening (10, then 4 cm); maize has no vascular cambium, so its thickening (6 to 22 mm) is from primary growth, while the bean base thickens slightly as the vascular cambium becomes active. Connect to hormones: auxin from the apical bud inhibits lateral buds, and cytokinins promote them (0 branches with the tip intact, 3 after removal); gibberellins promote germination and abscisic acid maintains dormancy.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) with a Gallery Walk. CER requires learners to connect specific data to a biological mechanism rather than just state facts. The Gallery Walk gives each explanation a real audience, and peer questions reveal gaps in reasoning before the final model is drawn.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review of the CER sheets with a short rubric: (1) a clear claim, (2) at least two data points with units, (3) correct scientific reasoning. Success indicator: at least 80% of groups include '8 of 20' or 'scarified, 7 germinated' for puzzle 1, and 'apical dominance, 0 vs 3 branches' for the branching question. Oral probing: listen for 'rain' as the explanation, which signals a lingering misconception. Teacher notes which groups confuse germination and emergence.

framework.learnerExperience: The class reviews the Driving Question Board built in Lesson 1 and updated in later lessons. Wanjiru reads each question aloud, and the class decides with a show of hands and a justification whether it is Answered, Partly answered or Still open, then moves the card to the matching column with a short evidence note (for example, 'What is growth and development?' is answered with the maize and bean stem width and the Lesson 2 definitions). Learners write a new question for the open column if their thinking has moved on (for example, 'How do farmers in Kitale reduce losses from waterlogged patches?' or 'Can gibberellin be used to speed up germination of old bean seed?'). Each learner completes an exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?'
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: 'Let us return to Wanjiru's first questions. Can we answer them now, and which card is our proof?' Read each question and WAIT 10-15 seconds before asking for a verdict. Cold-call 4 different learners to justify moving a card, and ask 'Who has a different view?' for at least 2 cards. Ask: 'Which question is only partly answered, and what would we need to find out?' Record unresolved questions for Lesson 10, such as the cost and income of the nursery. Collect the exit tickets and note learners whose answers list activities rather than evidence (for example, 'we did jars' instead of '18 of 20 germinated with water, air and warmth').
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning using the DQB. Sorting questions by status makes progress visible and shows learners that science is cumulative, and that new questions come from answered ones. It ties every earlier lesson back to the main question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit ticket with two prompts. Success criteria: the first answer names a specific data point and the second links it to the driving question. Oral probing during the DQB review: can learners give the evidence for moving a card? Quick quiz check (3 minutes, optional): 'Name two conditions necessary for germination; what is dormancy; which hormone maintains dormancy?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners take their Day 1 drawing and explanation. Using a different coloured pen, they revise it into a final model for Mr. Wafula's field. The model must include: (1) the maize and bean seed structures (scutellum and endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza versus two cotyledons, testa, micropyle, hilum, plumule, radicle); (2) the conditions for germination (water, oxygen, suitable temperature) with the waterlogged patch; (3) the causes of failure by crop (maize 5, 4, 3 and beans 8, 6, 4, 2); (4) hypogeal and epigeal emergence; (5) growth: primary growth at apical meristems, a sigmoid curve for each crop, stem thickening, and secondary growth in the bean base but not in maize; (6) hormones: auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid and apical dominance. Each learner adds a short caption: 'My Day 1 idea was..., and now I think... because...' Groups swap models for peer review, tick the checklist and suggest one improvement. Fast finishers add a note about how a farmer could improve germination: scarify hard-coated bean seed, use viable seed, avoid waterlogged patches, and protect seed from pests.
framework.teacherMoves: Madam Achieng says: 'Do not erase your Day 1 model. Use a new colour so that you and I can see how your thinking has grown.' Share the model checklist on the board. Circulate to check that learners show the cause of each type of failure separately and do not blur dormancy and non-viability. Ask: 'Where on your model does the rain appear, and what does your evidence say about its role?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners to explain one change from their Day 1 model. Remind learners that the outcome is: the seeds differ because of seed structure, seed condition and environment, not because of the rain or the planting date, and that hormones coordinate growth once seedlings are established. Close by previewing Lesson 10: 'Next lesson you will present this explanation and plan how to share and sell seedlings from our school nursery for conservation and income.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision. Comparing the final model with the Day 1 model lets learners see their own conceptual change, which supports Learning to Learn. Peer review of the models adds accountability and exposes missing links, such as the role of oxygen or the difference between maize and bean thickening.
framework.formativeAssessment: Model check using the checklist: all six components present, correct labels, causes of non-germination separated by crop with numbers adding to 12 and 20, and a written reason for each change. Peer review sign-off. Success indicator: at least 80% of learners correctly show dormancy (hard seed coat) as different from non-viability and explain apical dominance with the 0 versus 3 branches data. Observation checklist for unity: all group members contribute.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: (1) Could most learners separate dormancy, non-viability, pests and waterlogging with the right counts? (2) Did learners use evidence with units, or did they fall back on 'because of the rain'? (3) Did any group struggle to link hormones (apical dominance, gibberellin, abscisic acid) to the field observations? (4) Did the DQB review show new, deeper questions? (5) Which learners still confuse germination with emergence, or growth with development, and what small-group support do they need before Lesson 10? (6) Were the materials (cards, flip chart, chalkboard, printed tables) enough for the class size, and how would you adapt the group size next time? Note any learners who need extra help in explaining in simple scientific English.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that on Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale, maize H614 (88 of 100 germinated by Day 14, emerged Day 7, 125 cm by Day 42) and Rosecoco beans (80 of 100 germinated, emerged Day 8, 44 cm by Day 42) behaved differently even though they were planted on the same day after 25 mm of rain. Non-germinating seeds: maize 12 (5 pests/fungi, 4 non-viable, 3 waterlogged) and beans 20 (8 hard seed coat, 6 waterlogged, 4 non-viable, 2 pests). After scarification, 7 of the 8 dormant beans germinated.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned that the seeds differ in structure (maize is a monocot and hypogeal; bean is a dicot and epigeal), that germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature, that dormancy means a viable seed fails to germinate even in good conditions, that primary growth at meristems gives a sigmoid growth curve, that maize has no vascular cambium and no true secondary growth, and that hormones (auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid) coordinate growth, including apical dominance.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The differences came from seed structure, seed condition (dormancy, viability, pests) and the environment (such as the waterlogged patch), not from the rain or the planting date. Once growing, hormones coordinate growth: the maize grows taller and thicker through primary growth, while the bean branches only when the tip is removed, because auxin from the apical bud inhibits the lateral buds.

LESSONS.title: Presenting Our Final Explanation and Sharing Seedlings with Kitale
LESSONS.substrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
LESSONS.aresKeywords: final explanation, claim-evidence-reasoning, gallery walk, model comparison, driving question board, tree nursery, seedling sales, conservation, financial literacy, Wangari Maathai

slo.purpose: Learners communicate their final Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanation of why Mr. Wafula's maize H614 and Rosecoco beans differ in germination, emergence and growth, compare it with their Lesson 1 model, close out the Driving Question Board, and plan how to share and sell nursery seedlings for conservation and income.
slo.knowledge: By the end of the lesson, the learner should be able to: (1) explain that the maize and beans differ because of seed structure (maize monocot, hypogeal; bean dicot, epigeal), seed condition (8 dormant beans with hard coats, non-viable seeds, pest damage) and environment (waterlogged patch, no oxygen), not because of the rain or planting date; (2) explain that hormones (auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid) coordinate growth, and that primary growth at meristems lengthens shoots and roots while apical dominance explains why beans branch only when the tip is removed; (3) calculate the sales of 60 seedlings at KES 20 each = KES 1,200, less cost of KES 300, giving a profit of KES 900.
slo.skills: NGSS Science and Engineering Practices: Constructing Explanations (CER), Engaging in Argument from Evidence (peer review), Developing and Using Models (comparing Lesson 1 and final models), Obtaining, Evaluating and Communicating Information (gallery walk and presentation), Using Mathematics (profit calculation). Communication in simple, clear scientific English.
slo.attitudes: Values: Unity (working harmoniously in groups to prepare and present); Patriotism (devotion to the community by sharing seedlings for environmental conservation). Core competencies: Citizenship (solving community problems by sharing seedlings from the nursery); Learning to Learn (reflecting on own work and adjusting accordingly). PCIs: Financial Literacy (generating income by selling seedlings); Prevention of Global Warming (establishing a tree nursery and distributing seedlings in the community).
slo.keyInquiry: How does growth occur in plants? Driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the closing lesson of the storyline. Lesson 9 produced the final model by synthesising evidence from Lessons 1-8, and Lesson 8 produced the rooted cuttings for the nursery. Here learners present the explanation to peers, show how their thinking has changed since Lesson 1, finish the DQB, and turn their knowledge into community action, following the example of Dr. Wangari Maathai and the Green Belt Movement.
slo.safetyNotes: Wash hands after handling soil, seedlings and polythene tubes. Carry seedling trays with two people. Wear closed shoes in the nursery area. Handle cash in the mock sale only under teacher supervision and use play money or tally sheets. Do not taste any seeds, which may be treated with chemicals.

LESSONS.overview: Madam Achieng's Form 3 class returns to the puzzle from Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale: maize H614 and Rosecoco beans were planted on the same day, 3 cm deep, after 25 mm of rain, yet 88 maize and 80 bean seeds out of 100 germinated, beans emerged on Day 8 and maize on Day 7, and growth patterns differed. Learners first make a prediction about which parts of their Lesson 1 model were right. They then observe, in a gallery walk, the final explanations of other groups, and use a CER frame to explain the differences. Next they compare their Day 1 model with the final model and complete the DQB. Finally they plan how to share and sell the nursery seedlings: 60 seedlings of the best treatment (Aloe vera gel, 24 of 30 rooted, 80%) at KES 20 each gives KES 1,200, less KES 300 cost, a profit of KES 900. This links science to conservation, income and the example of Dr. Wangari Maathai.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Think-Pair-Share. Learners look at their Lesson 1 drawing and explanation of why Mr. Wafula's maize and beans behaved differently, which are pinned in their books or on the wall. Individually (2 min) they write a quick prediction: 'Which ideas in my Day 1 model do I think were correct, which were incomplete, and what would I now add?' They also predict: 'If our school sells 60 seedlings at KES 20 each, how much money will we make, and what will we spend it on?' They pair up with a partner (3 min), then 4 pairs share with the class. Expected ideas: 'I thought the rain or planting date caused the difference', 'I did not know about dormancy', 'I did not think about waterlogging or oxygen'.
framework.teacherMoves: Greet the class: 'Habari za asubuhi. Eight weeks ago we met Mr. Wafula's farm in Kitale. Same day, same field, same 25 mm of rain. Today we finish the story.' Display the phenomenon: 88 of 100 maize and 80 of 100 bean seeds germinated at Day 14. Ask: 'What did you think caused the difference on Day 1?' Give individual think time and WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before anyone speaks. Circulate and note 3 learners with different Day 1 ideas. Cold-call 4 pairs (not volunteers only): 'Wanjiru and partner, what was one idea you now want to change?' Do not correct predictions yet; record on the board under 'Day 1 ideas'. Say: 'Keep these ideas. At the end of the lesson we will see how far your thinking has moved.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share: individual thinking first ensures every learner commits to a position, pair talk lets quieter learners rehearse in a low-risk setting, and class sharing exposes the range of Day 1 ideas. This creates a clear baseline against which learners measure their growth in understanding by the end of the lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observation checklist: tick learners who (a) write a specific prediction not just 'it will change', (b) name at least one earlier idea such as rain or planting date, and (c) explain their reasoning to the partner. Oral probe: 'What made you think that on Day 1?' Indicator of misconception to note: learners still attributing differences to rain or planting date, or thinking healthy-looking seeds must germinate.

framework.learnerExperience: (25 min) Gallery Walk. Each of 6-8 groups of 5 learners (sharing materials) has prepared a poster or manila sheet in Lesson 9 showing: (a) labelled drawings of maize and bean seed structure (maize: scutellum, endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza; bean: two cotyledons, testa, micropyle, hilum, plumule, radicle); (b) the germination data (88 maize vs 80 beans out of 100, and the reasons for the 12 and 20 non-germinating seeds); (c) the conditions tests (jar results 18, 0, 1, 0); (d) growth data (heights, stem widths, root lengths and sigmoid curves); (e) hormones and apical dominance (0 vs 3 branches); and (f) their final CER explanation. Groups rotate every 4 minutes. Each learner carries a peer review card to record at each poster: one thing that is well supported by evidence, one question, and one suggestion. One presenter stays with each poster to explain it (rotating roles so that every member presents) while others visit. Learners check that numbers match the Mr. Wafula data: e.g. 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 maize failures; 8 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 20 bean failures; 7 of 8 scarified beans germinated by Day 7.
framework.teacherMoves: Before the walk, show the review card and the success criteria: 'A strong explanation names the claim, uses at least 3 pieces of numerical evidence, and explains the biology (reasoning).' Set a timer for 4-minute rotations and call 'Move on' clearly. As groups rotate, listen for accurate use of terms: germination (radicle emerges), emergence (shoot above soil), dormancy (viable seed that fails to germinate), viable. Ask presenters probing questions: 'Fatuma, why did 18 seeds germinate in the jar with water, air and 25 C but only 1 without air?' 'Otieno, how do your height data show maize is taller from Day 14 onward?' 'Kiprop, why did aloe perform best in the cuttings?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after each question. Cold-call at least 6 learners across the room. Where the data are wrong, do not give the right answer: ask 'Which table in the unit can you check?' If the electricity or the videos are not available, use the teacher-prepared stills of the bean and maize time-lapse (Bean Time-Lapse 25 days soil cross section; Growing corn time lapse) printed on A4 sheets placed beside the posters. Record 3 common errors for use in the next phase.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk with peer review: viewing multiple representations of the same phenomenon lets learners test their own explanation against others' evidence. Giving and receiving feedback with the criteria 'claim, evidence, reasoning' makes the standards for good scientific explanation visible and builds argumentation from evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Peer review cards collected and checked: indicators are that comments cite specific data (e.g. 'Your bean jar numbers 18, 0, 1, 0 support the need for water, air and warmth') rather than general praise. Observation checklist for practical communication skills: speaks clearly, uses labelled diagrams, uses correct terms such as scutellum, coleoptile, testa, epigeal, hypogeal. Teacher records misconceptions such as confusing germination with emergence, or saying maize has secondary growth.

framework.learnerExperience: (20 min) Claim-Evidence-Reasoning. Back in groups, learners finalise and present a 2-minute oral CER answer to the driving question: 'What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?' Claim: 'The differences are caused by seed structure, seed condition and environment, not by rain or planting date.' Evidence: they cite at least three data points, e.g. (1) Day 14 germination: maize 88, beans 80 out of 100; (2) non-germination causes: maize 5 pests/fungi, 4 non-viable, 3 waterlogged; beans 8 hard seed coat (dormant), 6 waterlogged, 4 non-viable, 2 pests; 7 of 8 dormant beans germinated after scarification; (3) emergence: maize coleoptile pierces the soil Day 7 (hypogeal, scutellum stays underground) and beans raise cotyledons above ground Day 8 (epigeal); (4) heights at Day 42: maize 125 cm vs bean 44 cm; stem width 22 mm vs 6 mm; (5) apical dominance: 0 branches with tip, 3 branches after the tip is removed at Day 20. Reasoning: they link the evidence to biology: the hard testa stops water uptake in dormant bean seeds; oxygen is needed for respiration so waterlogged seeds fail; the bean has two cotyledons that lift above ground while maize has a single scutellum that stays below; primary growth occurs at apical meristems, with maize's steepest log phase between Day 21 and 35 and bean's between Day 14 and 28; auxin from the tip inhibits lateral buds while cytokinins promote them; gibberellins promote germination while abscisic acid maintains dormancy. Each group then answers a 'what if' challenge from the teacher.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the CER frame: 'I claim that ... The evidence is ... This shows that ... because ...'. Say: 'Your explanation must be one that Mr. Wafula could use to improve his next planting.' Select 4 groups to present (each 2 min), choosing different learners than in the gallery walk. After each, ask the class: 'Who can add evidence?' and 'Who can challenge the reasoning?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds. Use these challenge questions, cold-calling 5 learners: 'If Mr. Wafula planted in the waterlogged low patch again, which seeds fail and why?' 'Why were 8 beans healthy-looking but did not germinate, and what should he do?' 'If he wanted branching in beans, what would you tell him?' 'Why does maize keep thickening without cambium?' Press for mechanism: 'You said hormones cause it; which hormone, and what does it do?' Correct remaining misconceptions explicitly using the data, for example if a learner says maize has secondary growth: 'What does the stem width data of maize, 6, 14, 22 mm, come from, and which meristem is missing?' Remind learners to use 'germination' and 'emergence' exactly. Allow learners to speak in simple, clear English; clarify terms such as scarification and viable.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: separating the three components forces learners to ground each claim in the Mr. Wafula data and justify the link with biological principles. Oral defence and challenge questions move learners from description to mechanistic explanation, and shared critique refines the class consensus.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a CER rubric with indicators: Claim is clear and answers the driving question (0-2); Evidence includes at least 3 accurate figures from the data (0-2); Reasoning links to structure, dormancy, oxygen, meristems or hormones (0-2). Oral probing identifies misconceptions about secondary growth in maize and confusion between dormant and non-viable seeds. A quick 3-question quiz on the board (cold-call): 'Define dormancy', 'Name the hormone that maintains dormancy', 'Which type of germination is bean?' Expected answers: viable seed that fails to germinate in favourable conditions; abscisic acid; epigeal.

framework.learnerExperience: (10 min) Learners return to the Driving Question Board. Wanjiru and a partner read out the Day 1 questions one by one (e.g. 'Why did some healthy-looking seeds not germinate?', 'What is growth and development?', 'Why did beans branch?'). Groups move sticky notes into three columns: 'Answered with evidence', 'Partly answered', and 'New questions'. For each answered question, a learner writes the key answer and the lesson where the evidence was found (e.g. dormancy and 7 of 8 germinating after scarification in Lesson 3; conditions in Lesson 4; sigmoid curves in Lesson 6; apical dominance in Lesson 7). Learners add at least one new question for the future, such as 'Which tree species would suit Kitale best for the nursery?' or 'How do other hormones such as ethylene affect fruit ripening on a farm?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'This board has followed us from Lesson 1. Let us see whether we have answered Wanjiru's questions.' Read each question aloud and ask, 'Is it answered? What is your evidence?' Cold-call 6 different learners. WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Probe: 'Which lesson gave us that evidence?' Where an answer lacks evidence, leave the note under 'Partly answered' rather than telling them the answer. Praise strong questions. Ask: 'Which question is the most important for farmers around Kitale, and why?' Take a photo or copy the final DQB onto manila paper for the class record if no camera is available. Link new questions to future learning.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discussion and questioning with the DQB: revisiting the original questions shows learners how each lesson contributed to the main question, makes the coherence of the storyline visible, and helps learners see what science still leaves open.
framework.formativeAssessment: Indicators: learners place questions in the correct column and justify with evidence from a particular lesson; at least 3 new, testable questions are posted. Observation: Wanjiru and others use the board to link lessons instead of recalling facts in isolation. Misconceptions flagged by notes placed incorrectly as 'Answered' without evidence.

framework.learnerExperience: (15 min) Model revision and community action planning. (a) (7 min) Each learner places their Day 1 drawing and explanation beside their final model from Lesson 9 and writes a short comparison: 'What I drew on Day 1', 'What I now know', 'The evidence that changed my mind'. They use a table with columns: Seed structure, Seed condition (dormancy, viability), Environment (water, oxygen, temperature), Growth type, Hormones. They label added features such as scutellum, coleoptile, testa, micropyle, shoot apical meristem, auxin from the tip inhibiting lateral buds, and a note on waterlogging in the low patch. (b) (8 min) In their groups they plan how to share and sell the school nursery seedlings in Kitale. Using the nursery results from Lesson 8 (30 cuttings per treatment: plain water 9 rooted, bulb onion 21, cinnamon 18, aloe vera gel 24 rooted, 80% best), they decide to sell 60 seedlings of the aloe treatment at KES 20 each. They calculate: income 60 x 20 = KES 1,200; cost of polythene tubes and soil KES 300; profit 1,200 - 300 = KES 900. They decide how to use the profit (for example, buying more tubes and soil for the next batch, or giving some seedlings free to a primary school), who to sell to (parents, farmers, church, market in Kitale), how to advertise a short pitch ('Plant a tree, protect our climate, as Wangari Maathai taught us'), and how to teach buyers to care for the seedling (watering, avoiding waterlogging, protecting from pests). They connect the plan to preventing global warming, as trees absorb carbon dioxide.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Place your Day 1 drawing next to your final model. Put a tick where you were right and a star where you changed.' Circulate and ask: 'What evidence changed your idea about the rain?' 'Where does your model show the dormant beans?' 'What does your model explain that your Day 1 model could not?' WAIT TIME 10-15 seconds. Cold-call 4 learners to share one change. Then introduce the plan: 'Dr. Wangari Maathai started with seedlings in Kenya and the Green Belt Movement planted millions of trees. We have 60 seedlings ready.' Ask them to check the arithmetic, then probe: 'Why is KES 20 a fair price?' 'Why not sell for less than the KES 300 cost?' 'How does selling a seedling help conservation in Kitale?' 'What should we tell a buyer about watering, given what we know about oxygen and waterlogged seeds?' Ensure the plan includes a role for each member (Kiprop as nursery lead, record-keeper, cashier, communicator, customer care), supporting Unity. If the class is large, give each group a different task (pricing, advertising, care instructions, record keeping) and combine them. Finish with the exit ticket: 'What evidence did we gather today?' and 'How does this help answer our driving question?' Collect and read these for reflection. Close with: 'You are no longer just learners, you are Kitale's tree growers.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision: placing the Day 1 model next to the final model gives learners concrete evidence of conceptual change and strengthens metacognition (Learning to Learn). Linking the model to the nursery plan shows that scientific understanding (oxygen, dormancy, hormones, rooting) guides real decisions about conservation and income.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Biology Grade 11: Growth and Development in Plants
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation for the driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants? Think back to Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale. He planted maize H614 and Rosecoco beans on the same day (Day 0), 3 cm deep, after 25 mm of rain. Use the evidence you collected in Lessons 1 to 10. Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use full sentences, include numbers from the data, and use the words germination, emergence, dormancy, viable, primary growth and hormones correctly. Where a prompt asks for Claim, Evidence and Reasoning, write all three parts. Where a data table is given, use it. Work on your own.

sections.title: Part 1: Seed structure and emergence (CER)
sections.prompt: Think about the time-lapse videos of the bean and maize seedlings that you watched. Write a Claim-Evidence-Reasoning explanation of how the different seed structures of maize H614 and Rosecoco beans lead to different ways of emerging. In your answer: (a) name the type of seed each crop has and how many cotyledons it has; (b) say where each crop stores its food; (c) use what you saw in the time-lapse videos to say what happens to the cotyledon(s) of each crop during germination and what this type of germination is called, and give the day each crop emerged above the soil; (d) explain the difference between germination and emergence.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Maize and bean seedlings emerge differently because their seeds have different structures. Evidence: Maize is a monocot with one cotyledon (the scutellum). It stores food in the endosperm, and the scutellum absorbs it. The coleoptile protects the shoot, and emergence was on Day 7. The bean is a dicot with two cotyledons that store the food. In the time-lapse, the bean radicle appeared on Day 3 and the bean emerged on Day 8, when an arched hypocotyl lifted the cotyledons above the ground. The maize radicle appeared on Day 4, and the scutellum stayed underground. Reasoning: Germination is when the radicle comes out of the seed. Emergence is when the shoot appears above the soil. They are different events, so a seed can germinate days before it emerges. In maize the cotyledon stays underground, which is hypogeal germination. In beans the hypocotyl arch lifts the cotyledons above ground, which is epigeal germination. The way each seedling reaches the surface comes from its seed structure and not from the rain or planting date, which were the same for both.

sections.title: Part 2: Why healthy-looking seeds did not germinate
sections.prompt:
Use the table from Mr. Wafula's field at Day 14 (100 seeds of each crop).

| Reason seed did not germinate | Maize H614 | Bean Rosecoco |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eaten or rotted by fungi/pests | 5 | 2 |
| Old seed with dead embryo (not viable) | 4 | 4 |
| Waterlogged low patch (no oxygen) | 3 | 6 |
| Hard impermeable seed coat | 0 | 8 |
| Total that did not germinate | 12 | 20 |

Write a CER explanation of why 12 maize and 20 bean seeds did not germinate. In your answer: (a) say which seeds were dormant and what dormancy means; (b) the 8 hard-coated bean seeds were later scarified and replanted as a separate re-test after Day 14. Say what happened to them and what this shows about the cause of their dormancy; (c) explain why the other failed seeds were not dormant; (d) name the hormone that maintains dormancy and the hormone that helps germination.
sections.exemplar: Claim: The seeds failed for different reasons, so dormancy explains only some of the healthy-looking seeds that did not germinate. Evidence: Only the 8 beans with a hard impermeable seed coat were dormant, and 0 maize seeds were dormant. These 8 were counted as not germinated at Day 14. In the later re-test, after they were scarified (nicked) and replanted, 7 of the 8 germinated by Day 7. The other failures were 5 maize and 2 beans eaten or rotted by fungi or pests, 4 maize and 4 beans with dead embryos, and 3 maize and 6 beans in the waterlogged low patch. Check: 5+4+3 = 12 maize and 8+6+4+2 = 20 beans. Reasoning: Dormancy means a viable (living) seed fails to germinate even in favourable conditions. The 8 beans were viable, and breaking the testa let them take in water, so the hard seed coat was the cause. The seeds with dead embryos were not viable, so they could never germinate. Seeds eaten by pests or rotted were destroyed. Seeds in the waterlogged patch were not dormant; their failure was linked to the lack of oxygen in that patch. Abscisic acid maintains dormancy, and gibberellins promote germination. So seed condition and environment, not rain or planting date, explain why healthy-looking seeds did not germinate.

sections.title: Part 3: Conditions needed for germination
sections.prompt:
Fatuma set up germination jars with 20 Rosecoco bean seeds in each jar. These are the Day 5 results.

| Jar | Conditions | Seeds germinated (out of 20) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Water + air + 25 C | 18 |
| B | Dry | 0 |
| C | No air (submerged in boiled, cooled water with oil layer) | 1 |
| D | Cold (fridge, 4 C) | 0 |

Write a CER explanation of which conditions a viable, non-dormant seed needs to germinate. Then use the table, and the numbers of seeds that failed in the waterlogged low patch of Mr. Wafula's field, to explain what may have happened there. Say how the jar and the field are alike and how they are different.
sections.exemplar: Claim: A viable, non-dormant seed needs water, oxygen (air) and a suitable temperature to germinate. Evidence: In Jar A, which had water, air and 25 C, 18 of 20 seeds germinated. When one condition was missing, almost none germinated: 0 in the dry jar B, 1 in jar C with no air, and 0 in the cold jar D at 4 C. Reasoning: Water activates the enzymes and metabolism in the embryo, and the stored food then supplies energy and materials for the growing radicle. Oxygen is needed for respiration to release that energy. A suitable temperature lets the enzymes work. If any one is missing, germination fails. In Mr. Wafula's waterlogged low patch, 3 maize and 6 bean seeds failed. Waterlogged soil has little oxygen, so the lack of oxygen is the likely reason, as jar C suggests, although we did not test the patch itself. The jar and the patch are alike because in both, a lack of oxygen is linked to seeds failing to germinate. They are different because the jar was a controlled test with 20 seeds and one condition changed at a time, while the patch was part of a field where we only counted the 3 maize and 6 bean seeds that failed and did not measure the oxygen. This shows that conditions in a particular spot in the field matter, not just the date or the rainfall.

sections.title: Part 4: Growth after emergence
sections.prompt:
After emergence the two crops grew differently. Use this data from Mr. Wafula's field (mean shoot height of 10 seedlings, in cm).

| Day | 7 | 14 | 21 | 28 | 35 | 42 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maize H614 | 3 | 12 | 30 | 62 | 98 | 125 |
| Bean Rosecoco | 4 | 9 | 18 | 30 | 40 | 44 |

Stem width at Day 14, 28 and 42 was 6, 14 and 22 mm for maize and 2, 4 and 6 mm for bean. Write a CER explanation of how the growth of maize and bean differ. In your answer: (a) say between which days each crop grew the most and how many centimetres it grew in that period; (b) say what shape a growth curve has and name the three phases, then say which phases you can see in the bean data and in the maize data up to Day 42; (c) explain what primary growth is and where it happens; (d) explain why maize gets thicker even though it does not make wood.
sections.exemplar: Claim: Maize grows faster than bean, and its growth was still rapid at Day 42, while bean growth had slowed by then. Both follow the sigmoid pattern of growth, but the data show different parts of it. Evidence: Maize was taller from Day 14 onward and reached 125 cm by Day 42, while bean reached 44 cm. Maize grew most between Day 28 and Day 35 (36 cm, from 62 to 98 cm), while bean grew most between Day 21 and Day 28 (12 cm, from 18 to 30 cm). Bean growth then slowed to 4 cm between Day 35 and Day 42. Maize still grew 27 cm between Day 35 and Day 42, which is less than the 36 cm before. Stem width rose from 6 to 22 mm in maize and from 2 to 6 mm in bean. Reasoning: A sigmoid growth curve has a lag phase, a log (rapid, exponential) phase and a stationary phase. Maize has its steepest growth between about Day 21 and Day 35, and bean between about Day 14 and Day 28 before flattening, so the bean data show a slowing towards the stationary phase. Maize is only starting to slow by Day 42 and still rises by 27 cm in the last week, so we cannot yet see a stationary phase for maize in this data. Primary growth is growth in length of roots and shoots. It happens at the apical meristems, where cells divide, then elongate, then differentiate. Maize is a monocot with scattered vascular bundles and no vascular cambium, so it has no true secondary growth and makes no wood. Its stem thickens through primary growth. Secondary growth by the vascular cambium happens in woody dicots such as Grevillea robusta, which show annual rings.

sections.title: Part 5: Hormones, apical dominance and your final model
sections.prompt: Mr. Wafula compared two groups of Rosecoco bean plants. In one group the shoot tip was left intact; in the other the shoot tip was removed at Day 20. Mr. Wafula counted the branches on each group at Day 25 and Day 32. (a) Using what you learned about hormones, write a CER explanation of what you would expect the two groups to look like and why. Use the numbers of branches from Lesson 7. (b) Name the hormone made in the shoot tip that affects lateral buds, say what it does to them, and name the hormone that promotes lateral buds. (c) Now write a short final answer to the driving question: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants? Finish by saying two ways in which your final model is different from your Day 1 drawing.
sections.exemplar: (a) Claim: The bean branched only when the tip was removed because the shoot tip stops the lateral buds from growing. Evidence: With the tip intact there was 1 main stem and 0 branches at Day 25. When the tip was removed at Day 20, 3 lateral branches grew by Day 32. Reasoning: The apical meristem makes auxin (IAA), which moves down the stem and inhibits the lateral buds. This is apical dominance. Removing the tip lowers the auxin, so cytokinins can promote the growth of lateral buds into branches. (b) Auxin is made in the shoot tip and inhibits the lateral buds, and cytokinins promote lateral buds. (c) The differences are not caused by the rain or planting date, which were the same for both crops. They come from seed structure (maize is a monocot with hypogeal germination and emerged on Day 7; bean is a dicot with epigeal germination and emerged on Day 8), seed condition (8 dormant bean seeds with a hard seed coat, plus separate failures from non-viable seeds with dead embryos and from pest damage) and the environment (water, oxygen and temperature, and the waterlogged patch). After germination, primary growth at meristems lengthens roots and shoots, and hormones such as auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins and abscisic acid coordinate growth and development. Growth is not only getting taller: plants also thicken, branch and change in form. My Day 1 model only said the differences might be due to the seed, soil, water, age or pests. My final model is different because I added dormancy and the hard seed coat, the three conditions needed for germination, the growth curve, and hormones such as auxin controlling branching.

SUMMARY_TABLE.subStrand: Sub-Strand 2.2: Growth and Development in Plants
SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: What causes the differences in germination, emergence and growth of maize and bean plants?

lessons.title: Meeting the Phenomenon: Mr. Wafula's Maize and Beans
lessons.observed: Maize H614 and bean Rosecoco were planted on the same day at Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale. The bean radicle came out on Day 3 and emerged on Day 8; maize radicle on Day 4 and emerged on Day 7. By Day 14, 88 of 100 maize and 80 of 100 bean seeds had germinated, so 12 and 20 did not, even though some looked healthy. Maize was taller from Day 14 onward, stems thickened, and the bean branched by Day 25.
lessons.learned: The two crops behave differently even with the same rain and planting day. Germination (radicle comes out) and emergence (shoot appears above soil) are not the same event. Growth is not only getting taller: stems also thicken and plants branch. We have many questions, such as what growth and development mean and why healthy-looking seeds do not germinate.
lessons.explained: Our first ideas are only tentative: we think the differences may be due to the seeds, the soil, water, age or pests, but we do not yet have evidence. Our initial models and DQB questions are our baseline, and we will revise them as we collect evidence. The next question is: What is growth and development?

lessons.title: Growth vs Development and Inside the Seed: Maize H614 and Rosecoco Beans
lessons.observed: We observed soaked Rosecoco bean seeds (testa, hilum, micropyle, two cotyledons, plumule, radicle) and maize H614 grains (one cotyledon called the scutellum, endosperm, coleoptile, coleorhiza, plumule, radicle). We also used Mr. Wafula's data: maize stem width 6, 14, 22 mm and shoot height 3 to 125 cm; bean stem width 2, 4, 6 mm and shoot height 4 to 44 cm.
lessons.learned: Growth is a permanent, irreversible increase in size or dry mass; development is a change in complexity and form through differentiation. Monocot (maize) and dicot (bean) seeds have different structures: the bean stores food in two cotyledons, while the maize stores food in the endosperm and one cotyledon (scutellum) absorbs it. Each part has a function, such as protection, food storage, and forming the root and shoot.
lessons.explained: Maize and beans differ in seed structure, which is part of why they emerge differently (maize by a coleoptile on Day 7; bean by an arched hypocotyl lifting two cotyledons on Day 8). Both seeds contain an embryo and a testa or coat, but the structure alone does not yet explain why some healthy-looking seeds did not germinate. This raises the next question: What is seed dormancy?

lessons.title: Seed Dormancy: Why Do Healthy-Looking Seeds Not Germinate?
lessons.observed: What we observed: Bean seed testa is hard; scarified seeds took up water faster than untreated ones. In Mr. Wafula's field at Day 14, 12 maize (5 pests/rot, 4 dead embryos, 3 waterlogged) and 20 beans (8 hard seed coat, 6 waterlogged, 4 dead embryos, 2 pests) did not germinate. 8 dormant beans looked healthy; 7 of the 8 germinated by Day 7 after scarification.
lessons.learned: What we learned: Dormancy is when a viable (living) seed fails to germinate even in favourable conditions. Causes include a hard impermeable testa, chemical inhibitors such as abscisic acid, and an immature embryo. Dormancy can be broken by scarification, soaking and other methods that match the cause. Dormancy helps wild seeds survive bad seasons but can delay germination on a farm. Not every failed seed is dormant: some are non-viable, eaten by pests or waterlogged.
lessons.explained: How this helps explain the driving question: Some healthy-looking bean seeds did not germinate because of a hard, impermeable testa (dormancy), while no maize seeds were dormant. So differences in germination depend on the seed's structure and condition as well as the environment, not on the rain or planting date. Other failures (waterlogging, lack of oxygen) still need to be explained, which raises our next question: How does germination occur?

lessons.title: Germination: Conditions Necessary and Types (Hypogeal vs Epigeal) in Maize H614 and Rosecoco Beans
lessons.observed: Jar results on Day 5 (20 Rosecoco bean seeds per jar): water + air + 25 C = 18 germinated; dry = 0; no air = 1; cold (4 C) = 0. Time-lapse: bean radicle Day 3, emergence (cotyledons above ground) Day 8; maize radicle Day 4, emergence (coleoptile pierces soil) Day 7, scutellum stays underground. Waterlogged patch: 3 maize and 6 bean seeds failed.
lessons.learned: A viable, non-dormant seed needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature to germinate. Germination is the radicle emerging; emergence is the shoot appearing above the soil. Maize shows hypogeal germination (cotyledon/scutellum stays underground) and beans show epigeal germination (cotyledons lifted above ground by the hypocotyl arch).
lessons.explained: Seeds on Mr. Wafula's farm differed because planting on the same day with the same rain does not give every seed the same conditions: the waterlogged patch had no oxygen, so 3 maize and 6 bean seeds failed, while seed structure explains the different emergence days (maize Day 7, bean Day 8). Together with dormancy (Lesson 3), these show that seed condition and environment, not the rain or date, explain differences. This leaves the question: How do plants show growth after emergence?

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Growth: Why Does Maize Thicken but Not Make Wood?
lessons.observed: We observed sections of maize, bean and Grevillea stems: maize had scattered vascular bundles and no cambium, bean had a ring of bundles with a thin cambium, and Grevillea had a thick ring of wood with annual rings. Maize stem width rose from 6 to 14 to 22 mm; bean rose from 2 to 4 to 6 mm.
lessons.learned: Primary growth at apical meristems lengthens shoots and roots. Secondary growth by the vascular cambium thickens woody dicots by adding secondary xylem and phloem and forming annual rings. Maize, a monocot, has no vascular cambium and no true secondary growth.
lessons.explained: Maize H614 is wider than Rosecoco bean because its stem thickens through primary growth, not because it makes wood. Only woody dicots like Grevillea thicken by secondary growth. This adds to the explanation of differences in growth between the two crops on Mr. Wafula's farm. New question: How can you measure growth in plants?

lessons.title: Measuring Growth: Regions of Growth and Growth Curves of Maize H614 and Bean Rosecoco
lessons.observed: Marks placed on maize and bean root tips spread apart most just behind the tip, showing growth occurs in a limited region. The height data for Days 7 to 42 showed maize H614 rising from 3 to 125 cm while bean Rosecoco rose from 4 to 44 cm. Maize increased most between Day 28 and 35 (36 cm) and bean between Day 21 and 28 (12 cm) in the table. Root length at Day 42 was 40 cm for maize and 26 cm for bean.
lessons.learned: Growth can be measured as height, stem width or root length. Growth in roots and shoots occurs at the apical meristem (cell division), followed by a region of elongation and a region of differentiation. A growth curve is sigmoid, with lag, log and stationary phases. Maize grows faster and for longer than beans, with its steepest growth between Day 21 and 35, while bean is steepest between Day 14 and 28 and then flattens.
lessons.explained: Maize and bean plants differ in growth, not only in germination and emergence, because they grow at different rates and for different lengths of time, even though they were planted on the same day in the same field. The curves show when growth is fastest and when it slows, but they do not explain what controls it. This raises the question for Lesson 7: Do we have hormones in plants?

lessons.title: Plant Hormones and Apical Dominance: What Coordinates Growth in Maize and Beans?
lessons.observed: We watched the video on major plant hormones and read about their roles. We looked at Mr. Wafula's bean data: with the shoot tip intact, 1 main stem and 0 branches at Day 25; with the tip removed at Day 20, 3 lateral branches by Day 32. We also recalled that 7 of the 8 dormant bean seeds germinated by Day 7 after scarification.
lessons.learned: Plant hormones coordinate growth and development. Auxin (IAA) is made in the shoot tip and promotes elongation while inhibiting lateral buds (apical dominance). Cytokinins promote cell division and lateral bud growth. Gibberellins promote germination and stem elongation. Abscisic acid maintains dormancy. Ethylene promotes fruit ripening.
lessons.explained: The bean with its tip intact did not branch because auxin from the apical meristem inhibited the lateral buds. Removing the tip lowered auxin, so cytokinin could promote lateral buds and 3 branches grew by Day 32. Hormones such as abscisic acid and gibberellins help explain dormancy and germination, so the differences between maize H614 and bean Rosecoco depend on seed structure, seed condition, environment and hormone coordination of growth.

lessons.title: Applying Hormones: Rooting Cuttings for the School Tree Nursery
lessons.observed: We observed that hibiscus or Duranta cuttings treated with natural sources rooted better than cuttings in plain water: out of 30 cuttings, plain water 9 (30%), bulb onion 21 (70%), Aloe vera gel 24 (80%) and cinnamon powder 18 (60%).
lessons.learned: We learned that a fair test changes only one variable and keeps others the same, that percentages let us compare treatments, and that hormones such as auxin at the cut base help cuttings form roots, so hormones can be applied in a school tree nursery.
lessons.explained: Aloe vera gel is the best treatment because 80% of its cuttings rooted compared with 30% in the control, and the only difference was the treatment. This shows hormones affect plant growth and development, which helps answer our driving question about why plants grow differently: seed structure, seed condition, environment and hormones all play a part.

lessons.title: Consolidating the Evidence and Building the Final Model: Why Did Mr. Wafula's Maize and Beans Behave So Differently?
lessons.observed: We observed that on Mr. Wafula's farm near Kitale, maize H614 (88 of 100 germinated by Day 14, emerged Day 7, 125 cm by Day 42) and Rosecoco beans (80 of 100 germinated, emerged Day 8, 44 cm by Day 42) behaved differently even though they were planted on the same day after 25 mm of rain. Non-germinating seeds: maize 12 (5 pests/fungi, 4 non-viable, 3 waterlogged) and beans 20 (8 hard seed coat, 6 waterlogged, 4 non-viable, 2 pests). After scarification, 7 of the 8 dormant beans germinated.
lessons.learned: We learned that the seeds differ in structure (maize is a monocot and hypogeal; bean is a dicot and epigeal), that germination needs water, oxygen and a suitable temperature, that dormancy means a viable seed fails to germinate even in good conditions, that primary growth at meristems gives a sigmoid growth curve, that maize has no vascular cambium and no true secondary growth, and that hormones (auxin, gibberellins, cytokinins, abscisic acid) coordinate growth, including apical dominance.
lessons.explained: The differences came from seed structure, seed condition (dormancy, viability, pests) and the environment (such as the waterlogged patch), not from the rain or the planting date. Once growing, hormones coordinate growth: the maize grows taller and thicker through primary growth, while the bean branches only when the tip is removed, because auxin from the apical bud inhibits the lateral buds.
